detail.abstract:
Privacy law relies on notice-and-consent regimes to govern data collection. This is premised on the idea that observed consent reflects users' underlying privacy preferences. Because consent is supposed to function as an informational signal, law assigns it the role of authorizing data collection. In practice, however, consent interfaces can make some options easier to recognize or implement than others, introducing asymmetric refusal costs that degrade the signal content of observed choices. We study this in a preregistered online experiment with German internet users (n= 1,142). Holding information and the formal option set constant, we vary cookie banner designs that differ in how refusal is presented: one visually emphasizes acceptance, one places rejection behind a settings menu, and one embeds the rejection option as a low-salience text link. We relate consent choices to privacy preferences measured via the IUIPC-8 scale, examining both the level of consent and the mapping from preferences to observed behavior. We find that users with stronger privacy concerns are consistently less likely to accept cookies across all designs. Two of the three designs generate large increases in acceptance relative to a neutral baseline; purely visual emphasis does not. 
We find no evidence that any design systematically weakens the preference-consent relationship. The dominant pattern is threshold relocation: interfaces shift aggregate acceptance through refusal-side costs without distorting preference-based ordering. To interpret heterogeneity across designs, we distinguish execution costs from recognition costs as distinct channels through which interface design shapes consent. Execution frictions primarily affect users with weaker privacy concerns; recognition frictions shift acceptance broadly, including among users with strong concerns. This distinction helps organize divergent findings across studies and has direct implications for evaluating consent as a signal of user preferences and for regulatory standards governing interface design.

title: Policing Police Violence: Sheriff-Coroners and the Underreporting of Police Killings. *
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics (ESE)

detail.title: Policing Police Violence: Sheriff-Coroners and the Underreporting of Police Killings. *
detail.abstract: In the United States, law enforcement kills three people per day, yet official statistics record only half. Using detailed geo-location of police killings and exploiting spatial and temporal discontinuities in medicolegal death-investigation systems across counties from 2000-2024, I show that sheriff-coroner jurisdictions are 15-19 percentage points (≈30 percent) less likely to report killings to the FBI. The effect concentrates among Black victims and increases after high-profile killings (Michael Brown, George Floyd), suggesting public scrutiny intensifies suppression rather than deterring it. The findings highlight how institutional dependence can systematically distort official record and hinder accountability.

title: The Revival of Industrial Policies in Developed and Developing Countries: The Mission-Oriented Perspective
affiliations: University of Dubrovnik

detail.title: The Revival of Industrial Policies in Developed and Developing Countries: The Mission-Oriented Perspective
detail.abstract: Industrial policy for a long time was treated as an anachronism in mainstream economics. That has changed in recent years. It has turned into the centre of policy discourse across both developed and developing countries. This paper examines the contemporary revival through the lens of the mission-oriented framework, which was principally associated with Mariana Mazzucato and extended by Dani Rodrik, Ha-Joon Chang, and Joseph Stiglitz. The paper traces the intellectual shift from the Washington Consensus market-failure paradigm toward a marketshaping conception of the state and surveys the major policy initiatives that embodied this shift. Beyond the literature review, the paper introduces the Semi-Parametric Markov Chain framework (Tolušić, 2026a), originally developed for regime identification in algorithmic foreign exchange trading, and applies it to industrial policy using the Juhász, Lane, Oehlsen, and Pérez (2025) dataset of 15,735 interventions matched with HS6 product-level export data from UN Comtrade across 20 products, 15 countries, and 21 years. The discrete-state SPMC analysis reveals three core findings. First, 11 of 15 countries show statistically significant Markov structure in instrument choice. Second, formal tests show that IP-targeted products experiencing high export growth have the same probability of maintaining that growth as non-targeted products: P(high growth next | IP+High) = 0.471 versus P(high growth next | NoIP+High) = 0.461, with the difference not significant (z = 0.314, p = 0.754). Third, a horizon scan on a balanced panel shows that Markov structure peaks at a 1-2 year lag and vanishes by 8 years. These findings suggest that IP targeting does not create detectable persistence in export growth outcomes at the product level, with the true effect bounded within 7 percentage points of zero.

title: Upgrading Housing: The Potential and Limits of Borrower-based Measures
affiliations: Council on Economic Policies, Magyar Nemzeti Bank, Latvijas Banka, Národná banka Slovenska, National Bank of Slovakia and Central Bank of Hungary

detail.title: Upgrading Housing: The Potential and Limits of Borrower-based Measures
detail.abstract: In this paper, we explore how borrower-based measures (BBMs) can be adjusted to provide additional funding for housing-related energy-efficiency investments without compromising financial stability objectives. We first show that lower energy costs and higher house price values resulting from renovation work allows an easing of borrowing limits while keeping loan risk metrics unchanged. We then focus on three recent easing measures implemented in Slovakia, Hungary, and Latvia and assess their effectiveness using a bank survey. We find that these policy changes did not significantly affect banks’ credit portfolio risk profile and thus financial stability. At the same time, they did not generate a significant increase in loans for energy-efficient investments. We thus suggest combining BBM adjustments with other policy measures to improve energy-efficiency in real estate.

title: Institutional Governance and the Direction of Global Capital Flows

detail.title: Institutional Governance and the Direction of Global Capital Flows
detail.abstract:
The global financial system confronts a structural paradox: countries with similar macroeconomic fundamentals and exposure to identical global financial conditions experience systematically different capital-flow outcomes. This paper argues that the missing variable is governance trajectory—the medium-run direction of change in institutional quality—which operates as a dynamic credibility signal through which investors price not merely where institutional systems stand, but whether they are strengthening or deteriorating over time.

The paper develops a conceptual framework linking institutional governance to cross-border capital allocation through credibility channels, and introduces the Institutional Governance Performance Index™ (IGPI™)—a composite of four World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators dimensions: regulatory quality, rule of law, government effectiveness, and control of corruption. Governance trajectory is operationalised as the five-year change in IGPI.

The empirical strategy is a two-way fixed-effects panel model covering 68 advanced and emerging economies from 2000 to 2024. A compound instrumental variable—exploiting variation in IMF programme entry driven by exogenous IMF liquidity cycles interacted with country-specific prior programme probability—addresses reverse causality. Data combine four publicly available sources: World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (2025 revision), IMF Balance of Payments Statistics, the U.S. Federal Reserve EFFR series from FRED, and the Cboe VIX index.

Results indicate that governance trajectory is statistically significant and economically material across all three capital-flow categories. A ten-point improvement in the five-year IGPI trajectory is associated with approximately 0.9 percentage points of additional FDI and 0.67 percentage points of additional portfolio inflows as shares of GDP—consistent with Alfaro, Kalemli-Ozcan, and Volosovych's (2008) benchmark that institutional quality is the leading explanation for the Lucas paradox. A moderation specification reveals that improving governance trajectories buffer economies against the global financial cycle: a ten-point VIX increase triggers portfolio outflows roughly half as large in high-trajectory economies compared to deteriorating-governance peers.

These findings carry direct implications for capital-flow management, macroprudential policy, and financial surveillance. The paper additionally introduces the Institutional Credibility Signal™ (ICS™)—a commercialisable governance-trajectory scoring instrument with a four-tier rating architecture designed for use by sovereign wealth funds, development finance institutions, and international financial institutions as a complement to existing macroprudential risk monitoring frameworks.

title: Social Media Algorithms as Information Intermediaries
affiliations: Brigham Young University - Marriott School, London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE), Brigham Young University and Texas A&M University - Department of Accounting

detail.title: Social Media Algorithms as Information Intermediaries
detail.abstract: We study how algorithmic content curation on financial social media shapes investor behavior and market outcomes. Using granular, user-level data on realized exposure to algorithmically curated content on StockTwits, we find that recommendation systems increase investor engagement and trading while crowding out attention to non-curated alternatives. Algorithmic curation appears to harm investor welfare, as it is associated with less informed retail trades and return reversals. These effects concentrate among users most susceptible to attention-driven trading and firms where this trading is most likely to move prices away from fundamental values. Findings are robust to alternative identification strategies, and extend to periods of major firm-specific news arrival. Our evidence demonstrates that algorithmically curated content appears to amplify uninformed, attention-driven trading in ways that erode the informativeness of retail order flow and impair market quality.

title: The Insecurity Triad (Part 1): Foundations of Convergence and Rival Sovereignty — An Analysis of Money, Land, and Mind (MLM)

detail.title: The Insecurity Triad (Part 1): Foundations of Convergence and Rival Sovereignty — An Analysis of Money, Land, and Mind (MLM)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research was conducted under the auspices of the Sundiata Post Intelligence Unit (SPIU). I am the Founder and CEO of Sundiata Post Media Ltd. No external funding was received for this study, and I declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
In this landmark inaugural paper, Max Amuchie, architect of The Insecurity Triad and the Trinity of State Decay theory, introduces the MLM Framework (Money, Land, and Mind) as a definitive analytical architecture for diagnosing the structural collapse of state sovereignty. Published as part of the Sundiata Post Intelligence Unit (SPIU) Working Paper Series, the study posits that kidnapping, banditry, and terrorism function as a synergistic "Insecurity Triad"—a convergence of mutually constitutive forces. This research contests conventional theories of "state failure," arguing instead that these forces produce a sophisticated structural contest over legitimate authority. By applying the MLM Framework, the author demonstrates how non-state actors do not merely create chaos; they establish a "Rival Order" by seizing control of illicit economic arteries (Money), territorial sovereignty (Land), and the psychological loyalty of the citizenry (Mind).

Drawing upon a rigorous theoretical genealogy—bridging the seminal insights of Ali Mazrui, Claude Ake, Achille Mbembe, Jean-François Bayart, and William Reno—the author situates this framework within the vanguard of African political thought while asserting its status as an original, predictive doctrine. While Nigeria serves as the generative case study, the framework’s logic is universal: it travels wherever these three forces coalesce to replace institutional governance with shadow sovereignty.

The paper argues that contemporary security discourse is fundamentally flawed, as it remains tethered to isolated threat categories that fail to perceive the convergent logic of modern insecurity. THE INSECURITY TRIAD provides the necessary corrective, offering an integrated strategic architecture that positions state recovery not as the repair of a "failed" entity, but as the deliberate production of a new political and security equilibrium.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Knowledge Accessibility, and the Democratisation of High-Quality Research
affiliations: , , Independent Researcher and Independent Researcher

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Knowledge Accessibility, and the Democratisation of High-Quality Research
detail.abstract: High-quality research has historically been produced under conditions of unequal access, not unequal access to information, which the internet substantially addressed, but unequal access to the intellectual practices through which ideas are sharpened, challenged, and made defensible. Those practices, adversarial debate, red teaming, and steel-manning, have required proximity to qualified interlocutors that most researchers, particularly those outside elite institutional environments and in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), have never had. Drawing on Bourdieu's (1986) framework of cultural capital and Merton's (1968) concept of the Matthew effect, this paper argues that artificial intelligence (AI) is the first technology to meaningfully change, at scale, the distribution of access to these practices. That change is real, conditional, and partial. It is real because the practices are now technically accessible where they were previously unavailable. It is conditional because realising their value requires AI literacy, intellectual disposition, and critical engagement with AI's documented limitations, including the sycophancy problem (Perez et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2023) and the hallucination problem (Ji et al., 2023; Maynez et al., 2020). It is partial because the legitimation of knowledge, whose research counts and why, remains concentrated in the same institutional structures as before. Against this backdrop, the paper identifies and analyses a structural contradiction we term the Paywall Paradox. Publishers have justified access restrictions on the grounds that peer review, editorial judgment, and institutional validation have value that should be compensated through access fees (Larivière et al., 2015). Critics have long contested this: peer reviewers are unpaid volunteers (Aczel et al., 2021), most research is publicly funded (Piwowar et al., 2018), and Elsevier's 37.1% operating profit margin, £942 million on £2.5 billion in revenues, is inconsistent with a cost-recovery rationale (Times Higher Education, 2019; SPARC, 2019; Larivière et al., 2015). That same research was then licensed to train AI without researcher consent or compensation: Informa projected £58 million ($75 million) in AI-related revenues for 2024 (Battersby, 2024); Springer Nature signed a $23 million deal with Google; Wiley signed a comparable agreement (Will Scott, 2025). This renders the process legitimacy argument structurally inconsistent. The paper also documents AI detection false-positive rates of 9% to 61.3% (OpenAI, 2023a; SurferSEO, 2026), the inconsistent landscape of journal AI disclosure policies, and the emerging open-access alternatives, particularly diamond open access, that represent the most coherent structural response to the Paywall Paradox. The paper concludes with specific, actionable policy recommendations for researchers, institutions, journals, and funders. This paper is a companion to Obasa and Obasa (2026a), which introduced Iterative Adversarial Inquiry (IAI); the Whetstone Method.

title: The Distributional Invariance of Steady-State Capital

detail.title: The Distributional Invariance of Steady-State Capital
detail.abstract: This paper studies the determination of steady-state capital in a broad class of intertemporal general equilibrium models with heterogeneous agents. We show that when investment is governed by a no-arbitrage condition equating expected returns to time preference and marginal productivity, the stationary capital stock is uniquely pinned down by primitives and is invariant to redistributions that preserve aggregate resources. The result holds independently of liquidity constraints, heterogeneous marginal propensities to consume, or incomplete markets, provided that distributional composition does not enter equilibrium return determination directly. The paper formalizes this distributional invariance property and characterizes the minimal structural conditions under which it fails. Distribution affects long-run capital only when it alters the equilibrium return condition, the investment mapping, equilibrium risk premia, or the feasible production frontier. In contrast, distribution may substantially influence transitional dynamics without affecting stationary capacity. The analysis provides a general structural criterion for distinguishing environments in which redistribution changes intertemporal adjustment paths from those in which it changes equilibrium capital itself.

detail.abstract: Everyone, including people with disabilities, has the right to a basic standard of living adequate for their own health and well-being and for their families including access to employment and decent work, financial services and economic resources, adequate food (freedom from hunger and access to nutritious food), clothing, clean water and sanitation (essential for health and hygiene), secure housing (safe, habitable shelter with access to services like water, sanitation and electricity and protection from displacement), health services (physical and mental well-being, particularly for vulnerable groups like children, mothers, and persons with disabilities), necessary social security (protection against economic shocks due to unemployment, disability, or old age) and services and education. The human right to an adequate standard of living is a cornerstone of international human rights law, enshrined in multiple instruments including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights to ensure that all individuals have access to resources necessary for dignity and health, and the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (“SDGs”) of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which were adopted by world leaders in September 2015 and went into effect on January 1, 2016, are intended to promote universal realization of these basic rights by mobilizing efforts to end all forms of poverty, fight inequalities and tackle climate change, while ensuring that no one is left behind.  The scope and expense of the activities associated with realization of these basic rights mandates that States act as the primary duty holders, particularly with respect to social security programs; however, businesses have an important role to play in these efforts and in so doing can foster innovation and stronger communities and empower women and members of other vulnerable groups.  Businesses can offer a unique set of resources that compliment and supplement the actions of States including financial support, human resources, technology and innovative problem-solving capabilities.  This work focuses on the contributions that businesses can make to the achievement of the SDGs by persons with disabilities, a group that includes about one in five people worldwide.

title: Vanilla Options: A Unified Mathematical Framework for Pricing, Hedging, and Volatility Modeling -A Comprehensive Review

detail.title: Vanilla Options: A Unified Mathematical Framework for Pricing, Hedging, and Volatility Modeling -A Comprehensive Review

detail.abstract: This paper provides a mathematically rigorous and unified review of vanilla options, encompassing pricing, hedging, and risk management for European and American calls and puts. The Black-Scholes-Merton framework is examined through three complementary approaches-the partial differential equation, risk-neutral martingale valuation, and Feynman-Kac formulation-revealing their conceptual equivalence and distinct practical advantages. A comprehensive sensitivity analysis covers all first-order and higher-order Greeks, demonstrating how Malliavin calculus provides efficient estimators where classical methods fail. American options are reviewed via free boundary formulations, variational inequalities, and numerical methods; least-squares Monte Carlo emerges as most versatile for high-dimensional problems, while finite difference methods remain preferable for precision. Volatility modeling is critically discussed, highlighting the trade-off between local volatility calibration accuracy and stochastic volatility's realistic forward dynamics. Practical challenges, including discrete hedging errors and transaction costs, are examined to bridge theory and tradable reality. By synthesizing over 150 derivations, this review establishes a unified framework, identifies persistent modeling tensions, and charts future research directions spanning machine learning, rough volatility, and quantum computation.

title: Structured GHG Disclosure Accessibility for Listed Japanese Firms: An Engineering Pilot Using EDINET and LLM-Assisted Report Extraction

detail.abstract:
We examine the accessibility of structured greenhouse gas (GHG) emission data for 89 major Japanese
listed firms using two complementary approaches: direct extraction from EDINET statutory filings,
and LLM-assisted extraction from voluntary sustainability and integrated reports. A post-extraction
audit of the cached EDINET iXBRL files found a mixed structured-disclosure state: 23 of the 89
firms contained CurrentYear GHG-related ix:nonFraction elements with unitRef and scale attributes
(including 17 with at least one Scope-specific standalone element, of which 12 contained a Scope
1 standalone element), while 19 contained only prior-year GHG-related structured elements and 47
contained no GHG-related ix:nonFraction elements under the inspected concept patterns. An initial
version of the extraction pipeline did not consume the unitRef and scale attributes and therefore
reported zero structured values; the corrected pipeline used in this version reclassifies the 89 firms
into structured-current-year, prior-year-only, and no-structured-tag categories. LLM-assisted extraction
was performed on voluntary PDF reports identified through prior or current acquisition for 88 of the
89 firms, producing 103 unique report-level records of which 63 contained at least one Scope value;
together these covered 52 firms, with Scope 1 values extracted for 49 firms. The voluntary-report
records exhibit three distinct schema-enforcement gaps on the voluntary-report side: only 11 of 49
firm-level Scope 1 records had units unambiguous from the voluntary-report record alone (14 of 49
once EDINET cross-reference cases are included); only 34 of 63 valid report-level records contained
explicit page citations; and source canonicality was not verified for any record. A fourth gap surfaced
as schema-shape and type-enforcement defects detected during pre-publication audit (a Scope 1 + 2 total
recorded in the Scope 1 field, a unit-unknown numeric value admitted unflagged, retrieval URLs stored
in a year field, and an LLM-emitted object-shaped value where a scalar was expected); a fifth gap is the
consumer-side schema-awareness gap on the EDINET side described above. In the four cases where an
explicit unit-labelled EDINET reference value could be matched to an LLM extraction, normalized values
fell within ±10% of the reference. The pilot suggests that the binding constraints lie less in document
reading itself than in unenforced schema requirements at multiple layers of the pipeline: structured
tags can exist without becoming accessible comparable data unless consumer pipelines consume the
attributes (unitRef, scale, contextRef) that make those tags meaningful, and LLM-assisted extraction
can produce candidate disclosure records but does not by itself yield comparable data. We argue
that comparable GHG data require schema-level enforcement on both sides of the pipeline: at the
disclosure side (consistent tagging of comparability-relevant fields) and at the consumer side (parsers
that consume and preserve schema attributes), together with unit normalization, evidence traceability,

title: Ending Shutdowns Forever: A Constitutional Amendment Proposal—Feasibility, Politics, and “Shutdown Insurance”

detail.title: Ending Shutdowns Forever: A Constitutional Amendment Proposal—Feasibility, Politics, and “Shutdown Insurance”

publicationDetails.detailsText: Thurgood Mashall Law Review (T. Marshall L. Rev.) Volume 50, Issue 2.

detail.abstract: The record-breaking government shutdowns of 2025 and 2026 have exposed a severe structural vulnerability within the American constitutional framework. Driven by rising negative partisanship, the modern appropriations process leverages the Antideficiency Act and the 1980 and 1981 Civiletti opinions to convert routine legislative gridlock into mandatory administrative paralysis. This Note argues that such shutdowns are fundamentally inconsistent with the Framers’ design for a continuously functioning national government, as they effectively grant the legislature an unconstitutional "suspending power" over the executive branch’s duty to faithfully execute the laws. To resolve this recurring institutional failure, this Note proposes the adoption of a Constitutional Continuity Clause to serve as embedded "shutdown insurance." Under this proposed amendment, if Congress fails to enact appropriations by the start of a new fiscal year, government operations would automatically continue at the prior year's funding levels for up to 120 days. Furthermore, by explicitly mandating the Secretary of the Treasury to prioritize and release these funds, the clause establishes clear judicial enforceability without infringing upon Congress's exclusive Article I "power of the purse." Ultimately, by outlining viable Article V ratification pathways and emphasizing bipartisan incentives, such as a stabilizing, status-quo fiscal baseline for conservatives and continuous funding of essential services for progressives, this Note presents a pragmatic structural repair to ensure the uninterrupted operation of the federal government.

title: A Time-Consistent Counterfactual Actuarial Runtime for Autonomous AI Agents

detail.title: A Time-Consistent Counterfactual Actuarial Runtime for Autonomous AI Agents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests. Computational experiments used Azure OpenAI services accessed under an institutional research sandbox; no commercial relationship influenced the design or reporting of the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a computational and theoretical study with no human or animal subjects, no human participant data, and no clinical intervention.

detail.abstract: We propose a runtime actuarial layer for autonomous AI agents in which every side-effect-bearing action carries a time-consistent, counterfactual risk toll computed against a contractually fixed safe default, inside an explicit underwriting boundary. The framework treats per-action insurance as the primary unit of analysis and replaces post-hoc annual liability cover with a pre-action transaction layer. The draft establishes four foundational results: (i) a well-defined counterfactual toll under a chosen safe-default mapping and continuation policy, with explicit non-uniqueness; (ii) a no-splitting property within an underwriting boundary that telescopes path-decomposed actions into a boundary potential, with a corollary tying gaming-resistance to boundary design; (iii) an irreversible-authority premium, split into a strictly positive action-level component and an if-and-only-if characterisation of the set-level robust capital increase; and (iv) a finite-sample conservative gating bound and a budget-recursion guarantee on the executed-action positive toll, with explicit caveats for online adaptive action selection. Each theorem is accompanied by a proof sketch isolating the assumptions used. A reference implementation in Python verifies the runtime engine end-to-end on a coding-agent database environment, with regression tests for two non-obvious failure modes: a loss-attribution error in which backup operations can mask the apparent loss from dropping a production table, and a gate-bypass error in which a priced action with a negative point estimate could skip the conservative envelope. Both failures are diagnosed in code and prevented by design.

title: It's Not Easy Being Green: Evidence on Corporate Green Bonds and Firm-Level Emissions Intensity
affiliations: Department of Economics, Columbia University

detail.title: It's Not Easy Being Green: Evidence on Corporate Green Bonds and Firm-Level Emissions Intensity
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether corporate green bond issuance is associated with subsequent reductions in firm-level carbon emissions intensity. Using a panel event study framework and a sample of 30 publicly traded non-financial firms issuing green bonds between 2018 and 2021, I analyze changes in combined Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions intensity across an event window spanning three years before to four years after issuance, controlling for firm and year fixed effects. While post-issuance coefficients trend consistently negative, none achieve statistical significance at conventional levels, and confidence intervals are wide across all event years. These findings provide limited evidence that green bond issuance leads to measurable operational decarbonization within the sample period, suggesting that green bonds may function more effectively as financing and reputational mechanisms than as direct drivers of firm-level emissions reduction. State-level socioeconomic heterogeneity among issuers and data limitations from third-party ESG sources contribute to the imprecision of the estimates.

title: Series I Bonds vs. USDC Stablecoin Yields: A Comparative Analysis of Inflation Hedging in the DeFi Era (2023-2026)
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Series I Bonds vs. USDC Stablecoin Yields: A Comparative Analysis of Inflation Hedging in the DeFi Era (2023-2026)
detail.abstract: This study compares Series I Savings Bonds and USDC stablecoin yields as inflation hedging vehicles for retail investors in the current digital asset era. Using monthly data from January 2023 through April 2026 (40 months), I derive I Bond composite rates directly from Consumer Price Index data and obtain USDC lending yields from Dune Analytics. The historical analysis reveals that I Bonds delivered an average annualized real return of positive 1.03% over the sample period, while USDC stablecoin yields delivered a marginal real loss of negative 0.06%. A $10,000 investment in I Bonds in January 2023 would have grown to $10,233 in real purchasing power by April 2026. The same investment in USDC stablecoin lending would have declined to $9,987, a difference of $246 in favor of I Bonds. I Bonds beat inflation in 85.2% of months, compared to just 48.1% for USDC. However, the gap narrowed considerably in 2025 and early 2026. In the first four months of 2026, USDC achieved a positive real return of 0.33%, slightly exceeding I Bonds' 0.20% over the same period. Volatility was low for both instruments, with I Bonds at 0.20% and USDC at 0.24% annualized. I conclude that while I Bonds have historically provided superior and more consistent inflation protection, USDC stablecoin yields have become increasingly competitive as DeFi lending markets mature. For investors willing to accept platform and smart contract risk, stablecoins offer a viable alternative with comparable inflation hedging properties and superior liquidity.

title: Tails of Two Sides-conditions Inspired by Thompson Sampling for Multi-armed Bandit that Lead to Further Understandings and Improvements
affiliations: Nanjing University, Nanjing University - School of Management and Engineering and Rutgers University, Business School, Department of Management Science and Information Systems

detail.title: Tails of Two Sides-conditions Inspired by Thompson Sampling for Multi-armed Bandit that Lead to Further Understandings and Improvements

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is nothing to declare here.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research does not involve patients/participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is not funded.

detail.abstract: We may understand a policy for the multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem as using a contest between arm-specific indices to select the arm to be pulled in each period. Any policy is identifiable by its coefficients that help to form the indices, with Upper confidence bound (UCB), as well as Thompson sampling with Gaussian priors (TSg) and Beta priors (TSb) being no exceptions. Inspired by the latter two, we formulate conditions on the coefficients that lead to tight regret bounds. These conditions basically propound an llrr principle: left tails should be light and right tails should be of the right size. They also guide us to pay particular attention to asymmetric Gaussian-indexed policies AGI(\sigma_l,\sigma_r) whose coefficients take the form-\sigma_l Z^_+\sigma_r Z^+ , with AGI(1,1) being just TSg. The latter's difference from the empirically more prominent TSb prompts us to generalize AGI further to AAGI policies that allow the magnitudes of index oscillations to depend on the various arms' potential rewards. Their good performances can be explained by another condition concerning a leading arm. Numerical experiments confirm that these policies, especially those with asymmetric tails, can perform well enough to beat TSb by large margins.

title: Nexion Energy Systems: Pre-Conceptual Design Specification -Hft-400

detail.title: Nexion Energy Systems: Pre-Conceptual Design Specification -Hft-400
detail.abstract:
The HFT-400 is a pre-conceptual design for a high-field, compact tokamak fusion reactor developed by Nexion Energy Systems. Designed to produce 400 MWth of fusion power and a net electrical output of 160 MWe, the system leverages high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets to achieve high power density in a significantly reduced machine volume compared to traditional ITER-class devices.

​The reactor's core technological innovations include:

  • ​High-Field Magnets: Utilizing yttrium barium copper oxide (YBCO) HTS magnets capable of reaching 20 T at the coil and 12 T on-axis, enabling a compact major radius of only 2.0 m.

  • ​Advanced First Wall: Implementation of a flowing liquid lithium (FLiLi) first wall to resolve solid component lifetime issues, provide intrinsic tritium breeding, and enhance plasma confinement.

  • ​Fuel Cycle: Deployment of deuterium-tritium (D-T) fuel with a target tritium breeding ratio (TBR) of >1.05 to ensure fuel self-sufficiency.

​The HFT-400 adheres to the NRC’s 2023 fusion licensing framework (SECY-23-0064), positioning fusion as a lower-hazard category than traditional fission. While the design builds upon established physics from programs like Alcator C-Mod and SPARC, critical uncertainties regarding liquid lithium stability and magnet joint reliability remain subjects for future experimental resolution. Economic projections estimate a first-of-kind levelized cost of energy (LCOE) between $90–$130/MWh, with a construction timeline of 8–10 years.

​Note: This specification is proprietary and requires a commercial license for deployment. Contact Dr. Sarah K. Whitmore at Nexion Energy Systems for research or licensing inquiries.

title: SISH: A Seshadri Inverse-Survival Halley Method for Implied Volatility and Greeks

detail.title: SISH: A Seshadri Inverse-Survival Halley Method for Implied Volatility and Greeks
detail.abstract: SISH reformulates Black-Scholes implied-volatility inversion as a fixed-iteration Halley problem in Seshadri log-survival coordinates, where the curvature identity $\sigma \cdot \mathrm{Volga}/\mathrm{Vega} = z_1z_2$ is algebraically exact. This coordinate choice avoids the relative-precision underflow that collapses price-domain solvers in short-maturity and deep-tail regimes. On a 1,080-cell boundary stress grid, SISH-8 records no observed underflow failures across implied volatility, Vega, Vanna, and Volga, compared with 108 failures each for the evaluated Jaeckel's Let's Be Rational (LBR-2) and Brent configurations. Terminal solver registers emit Vega, Vanna, and Volga with no measurable marginal latency in the reported benchmark. In a 1,000,000-point stochastic stress test, SISH-8 and LBR-2 agree within $10^{-5}$ on 99.28\% of the well-conditioned stratum; in flat-vega strata, price residuals define inversion success more reliably than volatility-coordinate deviations. Listed-market SPY and SPX experiments show repricing parity within bid-ask spreads while SISH preserves finite nonzero coordinates in boundary contracts where price-domain/reference paths return zero volatility. In heterogeneous CUDA batches, SISH-4 reduces timing expansion relative to the evaluated source-faithful LBR-2 CUDA port, while LBR-2 retains lower homogeneous scalar latency. These results position SISH as a tail-stable, Greek-native inversion kernel for risk engines where boundary sensitivity and heterogeneous throughput matter more than isolated scalar latency.

title: Why Organizations Need Continuous Security Auditing — Not Annual Compliance Checks
affiliations: European Institute of Management & Technology (EIMT)

detail.title: Why Organizations Need Continuous Security Auditing — Not Annual Compliance Checks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal conflicts of interest that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or experimental procedures requiring institutional ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Modern organizations increasingly operate within highly interconnected and continuously evolving digital environments where cyber threats develop rapidly across cloud systems, remote infrastructures, artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled ecosystems, and third-party operational environments. Despite this reality, many organizations continue to rely heavily on periodic cybersecurity auditing approaches primarily driven by annual compliance requirements.

While frameworks such as ISO/IEC 27001, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF), GDPR, and related regulatory standards remain essential for governance, accountability, and operational trust, periodic assessments alone are increasingly insufficient for maintaining effective cyber resilience within dynamic digital ecosystems.

This paper examines the growing importance of continuous security auditing as a proactive cybersecurity governance approach capable of improving operational visibility, ongoing risk awareness, governance integration, and adaptive resilience across modern digital infrastructures. The paper further explores the accessibility challenges faced by organizations, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), and discusses how lightweight continuous auditing approaches may contribute to strengthening cybersecurity governance, compliance readiness, and operational resilience.

title: Measuring Exposure to Institutional Decision Authority: A Trajectory-Based Framework for Administrative Governance

detail.title: Measuring Exposure to Institutional Decision Authority: A Trajectory-Based Framework for Administrative Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article does not involve human subjects research, identifiable individual-level data, or clinical experimentation. Institutional Review Board approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Existing approaches to evaluating automated and semi-automated decision systems focus on point-in-time assessments of accuracy, bias, and outcomes—treating decisions as discrete events rather than components of ongoing institutional interactions. This paper introduces Differential Authority Exposure (DAE), a formal measurement framework that shifts the unit of analysis from isolated decision events to cumulative exposure trajectories. DAE specifies five structural dimensions through which institutional decision authority is allocated and repeated across time: decision frequency, duration under authority, consequential intensity, repetition without informational resolution, and contestability deficit. All dimensions are operationalizable from routine administrative records—including transaction logs, status codes, notices, and appeals data—without requiring access to underlying algorithmic models.

The framework is illustrated using Medicaid work requirements, a policy environment characterized by repeated eligibility verification, automated data cross-checking, and provisional status transitions. DAE renders these exposure dynamics observable and comparable across institutional designs, enabling analysis of how administrative systems allocate decision authority across populations even when statutory rules and eligibility criteria are held constant.

By formalizing exposure as a measurable property of institutional design rather than isolated determinations, DAE extends existing approaches to algorithmic accountability and administrative burden, and provides a foundation for empirical analysis of how governance design shapes participation continuity, procedural stability, and differential exposure under repeated administrative interaction.

title: Historical-institutional Evolution of Entrepreneurship in Chile, 1970-2025: Economic Reforms, Public Policy, and the Entrepreneurial Ecosystem

detail.title: Historical-institutional Evolution of Entrepreneurship in Chile, 1970-2025: Economic Reforms, Public Policy, and the Entrepreneurial Ecosystem

contentFormat.other: Narrative review with a historical-institutional approach

detail.abstract: This article analyzes the historical-institutional evolution of entrepreneurship in Chile from 1970 to 2025, incorporating prior antecedents related to industrialization, family business, the developmental state, and the creation of CORFO. Through a narrative review of academic literature, institutional documents, and reports from national and international organizations, the article argues that Chilean entrepreneurship has moved from traditional, commercial, family-based, and adaptive forms toward a more institutionalized, globalized, and innovation-oriented ecosystem. The analysis organizes this trajectory into four periods: antecedents and the formation of productive capabilities until 1970; economic reforms, openness, and business reconfiguration from 1970 to 1989; democracy, growth, SMEs, and promotion policies from 1990 to 2009; and dynamic entrepreneurship, Start-Up Chile, digitalization, and contemporary challenges from 2010 to 2025. The article concludes that Chile has built one of the most visible entrepreneurial ecosystems in Latin America, but still faces structural tensions in financing, productivity, decentralization, technological sophistication, R&D transfer, and firm scaling. The agenda toward 2030 requires moving from mass firm creation toward an entrepreneurial strategy focused on innovation, productivity, territorial inclusion, and sustainable growth.

title:
Unified Feedback P&L and Grassmannian Recalibration Obstruction under Endogenous Covariation 

A Representation-Theoretic Invariance with Analytic and Geometric Corollaries
affiliations: and Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne

detail.title:
Unified Feedback P&L and Grassmannian Recalibration Obstruction under Endogenous Covariation 

A Representation-Theoretic Invariance with Analytic and Geometric Corollaries
detail.abstract:
When hedge flow moves the instruments being hedged, the covariance entering carry P&L is an endogenous clearing output rather than an external input. We prove a pathwise decomposition separating feedback amplification from ordinary benchmark-covariance error. If c Y is the realized traded-coordinate covariation, c Z is the latent no-impact covariation, and J = (I − B) −1 is the clearing resolvent, then
1 2 Z T 0 Ht : (c Y t − bct) dt = − 1 2 Z T 0 (J ⊤ t HtJt − Ht) : c Z t dt + 1 2 Z T 0 Ht : (bct − c Z t ) dt. 
The first term is pure feedback, determined by the dual congruence action of the resolvent on the book Hessian; the second is misspecification of the latent no-impact covariance. The same invariance of the Frobenius pairing simultaneously yields the Layer-1 self-financing identity, the clearing law c Y = JcZJ ⊤, and the factor-class recalibration test. For a factor class M(G), feedback is absorbable exactly when J col(G) = col(G); otherwise it creates structural leakage outside the factor span. We quantify this leakage by an exact Frobenius projection formula and a principal-angle lower bound, and we provide contraction, sensitivity, low-rank, propagator-limit, and numerical diagnostics for assembling and auditing the loop gain B = DQΛ DyΦ.

title: Liminal Perception, Ambiguity Tolerance, and Epistemic Stability in Human–AI Interaction

detail.title: Liminal Perception, Ambiguity Tolerance, and Epistemic Stability in Human–AI Interaction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This exploratory conceptual note develops a hypothesis concerning possible relations hips between liminal perception, ambiguity tolerance, and stable human–AI interaction. The initial observation emerged from a discussion about violet and ultraviolet light: vio let occupies the edge of the visible spectrum, while ultraviolet radiation remains physi cally real and effective despite being inaccessible to direct human perception. These phenomena were interpreted not merely as aesthetic curiosities, but as examples of partially representable realities situated at the boundary between physical presence, cognitive construction, and perceptual limitation. 

The paper does not argue that color preference predicts AI competence, nor does it propose any form of psychological classification based on aesthetic taste. Instead, it ex plores whether sensitivity to liminal perceptual phenomena may correlate with cognitive dispositions relevant to interaction with probabilistic AI systems. Such dispositions may include ambiguity tolerance, metacognitive awareness, structural pattern recognition, and the ability to maintain epistemically incomplete states without premature closure. 

The note further proposes that advanced human–AI interaction may depend less on purely technical prompting skills and more on stable cognitive interaction modes capable of operating under uncertainty, partial representation, and emergent system behavior. Violet and ultraviolet perception are therefore treated as heuristic entry points into a broader question concerning perceptual variability, probabilistic cognition, and interac tional stability in long-term human–AI systems. 

The paper is intended as a conceptual contribution to ongoing discussions of human–AI interaction rather than as an empirical study, psychological classification framework, or design methodology.

This document is explicitly exploratory and non-empirical. Its primary purpose is to pre serve the original conceptual architecture, define methodological boundaries, and out line a possible future research agenda.

title: Performance Substitutability in ESG Pay
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - Faculty of Business Administration (Munich School of Management) and LMU Munich School of Management

detail.title: Performance Substitutability in ESG Pay

publicationDetails.detailsText: TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency Working Paper Series No. 237
publicationDetails.journalName: TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examines how the substitutability of ESG performance for financial performance in executive compensation contracts relates to firm outcomes. Using hand-collected data, we distinguish between high-and low-substitutability contracts. In high-substitutability contracts, executives can receive bonuses for ESG performance alone. In low-substitutability contracts, ESG bonuses are contingent on meeting financial thresholds. We find that, on average, ESG pay improves ESG performance. However, this effect is concentrated among highsubstitutability contracts, whereas low-substitutability contracts show no significant improvement in ESG performance. We also find that high-substitutability contracts are associated with weaker short-term financial performance, whereas low-substitutability contracts preserve financial outcomes. A mediation analysis shows that high-substitutability contracts are more likely to include quantifiable and collectively applied ESG metrics, which partially explains their positive association with ESG performance.

title: The P behind Q: Empirical Evidence from Physical Drift in Put-call Parity

detail.title: The P behind Q: Empirical Evidence from Physical Drift in Put-call Parity
detail.abstract: Put–call parity is a terminal-payoff identity, but its enforcement is capital-using. I study the carry gap, the annualized wedge between option-implied and OIS discount factors, in SPX and RUT index options. Quoted parity is tightly compressed, while the synthetic–traded forward channel leaves a systematic wedge. I interpret this wedge as an implementation premium under finite arbitrage capital. A drift-preserving GBM term, rµτ, improves in-sample and leave-one-year-out fit, especially in SPX. The evidence suggests that physical drift enters not option payoffs, but the process enforcing risk-neutral parity.

title: An Entrepreneurial Ecosystem Framework for Economic Zones: Conceptual Map of Core Variables and Statistical Associations
affiliations: Maalexi Inc.

detail.title: An Entrepreneurial Ecosystem Framework for Economic Zones: Conceptual Map of Core Variables and Statistical Associations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Self

detail.abstract:
Despite their widespread use as instruments of structural transformation, Special Economic Zones (SEZs) remain theoretically underleveraged in the entrepreneurship literature and largely absent from the quantitative empirical base needed to identify the conditions that drive zone dynamism. Existing research has predominantly treated zones as policy objects—focusing on incentives, regulatory design, and location—while paying limited attention to the ecosystem conditions that shape their capacity to generate and sustain entrepreneurial activity. This study addresses that gap.

The research develops and empirically examines an eighteen-variable Entrepreneurial Ecosystem Framework for Economic Zones (EEF-EZ), integrating Isenberg’s (2011) ecosystem typology with variables derived from the SEZ empirical literature and urban economics. The framework is assessed through a purposive multi-country survey of 83 senior practitioners across 23 countries, representing approximately 55% of global SEZ activity. The analysis captures practitioner perceptions of variable relevance and is therefore positioned as exploratory.

Factor analysis and regression techniques identify three latent structural dimensions—Capital, Stabilisation, and Institutional—accounting for 67.25% of total variance. Nine variables emerge as high-salience, exhibiting strong and consistent associations across contexts, while others display weaker or more context-dependent patterns. These findings suggest an underlying ecosystem logic to zone design that extends across regulatory environments.

This study makes two contributions. First, it provides an empirically grounded account of how practitioners prioritise ecosystem conditions in the design, governance, and financing of SEZs. Second, it establishes a structured variable framework to guide future causal research linking ecosystem conditions to objective zone-level performance. Positioned as the first stage of a broader research programme, the study lays the foundation for subsequent work testing the impact of these variables on SEZ outcomes.

title: Influence of Social Media on Retail Investor behaviour in India: A Review
affiliations: Acropolis Institute of Management Studies & Research, Indore

detail.title: Influence of Social Media on Retail Investor behaviour in India: A Review
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of social media platformsincluding Twitter/X, YouTube, Reddit, and Telegramhas fundamentally reshaped the information landscape for retail investors in India. Following the surge in retail participation on platforms like Zerodha, Groww, and Upstox between 2020 and 2024, this paper examines how social media influences investment decision-making, risk perception, and market behaviour among individual investors. Drawing on a review of 8 published studies from 2019 to 2024, this paper finds that social media sentiment has a statistically significant short-term impact on stock price volatility, that financial influencers ("finfluencers") substantially affect retail investment choicesparticularly among first-time investorsand that information overload and herding behaviour represent significant risks in this environment. The paper concludes with recommendations for financial literacy policy and suggests areas for future empirical research specific to the Indian context.

title: Rigid Institutions, Irreversible Technology
affiliations: University of Hong Kong (HKU), HKU Business School and Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Rigid Institutions, Irreversible Technology
detail.abstract: Why are rigid institutions sometimes reformed without crisis? We develop a framework of technology-induced institutional change centered on two forces: institutional rigidity, whereby status-quo beneficiaries can coordinate to block direct reform, and technological irreversibility, whereby a new technology, once adopted, cannot be costlessly unwound. Facing institutional rigidity, a reform-minded government can pursue change indirectly by promoting an irreversible new technology. Decentralized adoption and dispersed information create strategic uncertainty: each incumbent who receives a sufficiently favorable private signal finds it individually rational to adopt, for fear of being stranded on the losing side, even though collective resistance would leave every incumbent better off. This splits the incumbent class, making the technology viable at scale and reshaping the political landscape: adopters, locked in, cannot profit without reform; new actors, spawned by the technology, cannot thrive without reform; and resisters, their rents already eroded, lack the incentive to fight. At a tipping point, reform becomes irresistible, ratifying the new economic reality. Empirically, agricultural mechanization in China causally increased land consolidation at scales incompatible with the household-based tenure system, followed by nationwide land-rights reform. The framework also explains uneven reform across sectors in high-rigidity settings.

title: What Truly Drives Greenwashing? Evidence from a Systematic Literature Review
affiliations: University of York and University of York

detail.title: What Truly Drives Greenwashing? Evidence from a Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract: Greenwashing (or ESG washing) is a growing concern in sustainability reporting literature, yet existing research remains fragmented on what drives it and overly focused on statistical significance rather than economic relevance. This study systematically reviews empirical evidence on the drivers of greenwashing and assesses their relative importance using measures of economic significance. We categorise drivers into motivators and inhibitors across internal and external dimensions. While numerous factors are found to be statistically significant, only a few show economically meaningful effects, namely market-based incentives, executive and board diversity, and CSR governance. This review also identifies key methodological limitations, including inconsistent reporting practices, overreliance on statistical significance and beta coefficients, and the use of narrow proxy measures for a multidimensional concept. We conclude by outlining directions for future research, highlighting underexplored drivers and calling for more integrated and rigorous approaches to understanding what motivates and constrains greenwashing.

title: The supply chain spillovers of private equity buyouts
affiliations: KU Leuven - Faculty of Economics and Business and

detail.title: The supply chain spillovers of private equity buyouts
detail.abstract: We study how private equity (PE) buyouts propagate through supply chains using unique firm-to-firm transactions data from Belgium. In normal times, suppliers of PE-backed firms outperform their peers by 5%–10% in employment and sales growth, primarily due to increased input demand from PE-backed customers rather than knowledge spillovers or other mechanisms. In economic downturns, however, this outperformance is attenuated and suppliers compress markups by around 8% as PE investors intensify bargaining pressure and reconfigure supply chains to extract cost savings. Beyond the direct effects on suppliers, we show that as PE-backed firms absorb supplier capacity, they crowd out competitors that rely on the same suppliers. Overall, our findings underscore that supply chains are central to how PE investors create and redistribute value.

title: Determinants and Strategic Solutions for Rice Export Expansion from Long An Province to the Philippine Market: A Subnational Analysis from Vietnam's Mekong Delta

detail.title: Determinants and Strategic Solutions for Rice Export Expansion from Long An Province to the Philippine Market: A Subnational Analysis from Vietnam's Mekong Delta
detail.abstract:
This paper investigates the determinants of, and strategic solutions for, rice export expansion from Long An Province-Vietnam's fourth-largest rice-exporting locality-to the Philippine market, which was the world's largest rice importer in 2010 (2.39 million metric tons). Employing a mixed-methods framework that integrates value-chain mapping, SWOT analysis and comparative competitive analysis, the study draws on secondary data spanning 2000-2011 from Vietnamese and Philippine government agencies, international commodity databases and bilateral trade records. Data cover 2000-2011; post-2011 regulatory changes are discussed in the Limitations section.
The empirical analysis reveals that Long An's rice export volume to the Philippines grew substantially after 2004, driven by structural demand deficits in the Philippines (domestic production averaging 10.7 million metric tons per year while consumption reached 15.2 million metric tons by 2010), a complementary bilateral political relationship codified in eight bilateral agreements, and Vietnam's competitive positioning as a cost-efficient supplier of 5–10% broken-rice relative to Thai rivals. However, the study also documents five critical structural constraints: (i) absence of internationally recognised rice brands; (ii) fragmented intermediary-based procurement limiting farm-gate quality control; (iii) post-harvest technology gaps (loss rates exceeding 12%); (iv) price dependence on Philippine National Food Authority (NFA) governmentto-government procurement channels; and (v) escalating competition from Thai, Cambodian and emerging private-sector importers.
The paper proposes a phased strategic roadmap (2012–2020) combining organizational reform, quality upgrading toward GAP and ISO certification, value-chain integration through a 'four-party linkage' (government–scientist–enterprise–farmer) model, targeted market development supported by e-commerce and trade promotion infrastructure, and macroeconomic policy recommendations on exchange-rate stabilization and export credit. The framework contributes a replicable subnational agricultural export strategy applicable to other Mekong Delta provinces and analogous rice-exporting regions across Southeast Asia.

title: From Summer to Spring: A Shift in US Housing Market Seasonality
affiliations: University of Cambridge and Cardiff University - Cardiff Business School - Economics Section

detail.title: From Summer to Spring: A Shift in US Housing Market Seasonality
detail.abstract: The US housing market exhibits pronounced seasonal cycles: prices and sales rise through spring, peak in summer, and decline through autumn and winter. Since 2021, this pattern has shifted earlier in the calendar year, with spring strengthening at the expense of the traditional summer peak. A leading explanation for housing market seasonality is the search-and-matching model of Ngai and Tenreyro (2014), which links these cycles to household mobility through a thick-market mechanism. In this framework, periods with higher mobility generate thicker markets and higher prices and transaction volumes. Viewed through this lens, a shift in the seasonal cycle of prices and sales raises the question of whether the timing of household moves has changed. Did residential mobility shift earlier in the calendar year after 2021? We find that it did. Using SIPP data, and corroborating evidence from Google Trends indicators, we document a post-2021 shift in mobility toward spring. We extend the model to a monthly frequency, prove the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium, and calibrate it to the observed mobility patterns. The calibrated model reproduces the spring shift in both prices and transaction volumes, consistent with the view that a change in the timing of household mobility alone can account for the recent shift in housing market seasonality.

title: Overconfidence and Endogenous Contract Incompleteness in Public Good Production
affiliations: Konan University

detail.title: Overconfidence and Endogenous Contract Incompleteness in Public Good Production
detail.abstract: This study examines endogenous contract incompleteness in a public good property rights model in which agents are overconfident about their ex-post bargaining shares. We show that unlike in the private good benchmark, sufficiently strong overconfidence does not necessarily make incomplete contracts mutually preferable to a fair complete-contract benchmark. Intuitively, public good benefits may be preserved even in a disagreement, which weakens the negotiation surplus channel through which overconfidence increases perceived investment returns. Incomplete contracting is mutually preferred only when disagreement remains sufficiently consequential and the relative investment technology satisfies suitable conditions.

title: TARGET2 Imbalances as a Settlement Substitute: Interbank Market Fragmentation and Financial Stress in the Euro Area

detail.title: TARGET2 Imbalances as a Settlement Substitute: Interbank Market Fragmentation and Financial Stress in the Euro Area
detail.abstract: This paper examines TARGET2 imbalances in relation to the slowdown of the euro area overnight interbank market and the transformation of the Eurosystem's operational framework after the global financial crisis and the European sovereign debt crisis. It argues that TARGET2 imbalances are not merely technical by-products of Eurosystem balance-sheet expansion, but balance-sheet traces of a structural reorganization of liquidity circulation inside the euro area. The paper develops and tests a substitution hypothesis: when private cross-border redistribution of central-bank liquidity through the overnight interbank market weakens, public settlement through TARGET2 increasingly records liquidity flows no longer intermediated through private money markets. Using a vector autoregressive framework for the euro area, the analysis links TARGET2 dynamics to overnight interbank market activity, the overnight money-market rate, and the Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress. The results show that positive shocks to TARGET2 imbalances generate a significant and persistent contraction in overnight interbank transaction volume, while financial-stress shocks generate an immediate and durable increase in TARGET2 imbalances. A separate transmission analysis further shows that TARGET2 is the most persistent balance-sheet response to excess-liquidity shocks among the variables considered, exhibiting a larger and more durable response than sovereign bond yields, equity prices, or bank lending. Finally, threshold results indicate that the center-periphery confidence gap becomes an active driver of TARGET2 accumulation only in the abundant-reserves regime, linking settlement dynamics to safe-asset scarcity and incomplete financial integration. The findings imply that TARGET2 should be interpreted not only as an accounting counterpart of central-bank operations, but also as a signal of impaired private liquidity circulation, financial fragmentation, and the evolving operational architecture of the Eurosystem.

title: External finance premium: market finance versus bank finance

detail.title: External finance premium: market finance versus bank finance
detail.abstract: This paper is the first to simultaneously examine firms’ market-based and bank-based external finance premia and investigate the behavior of corporate bond markets in the United States and the euro area, with a focus on country- and state-level heterogeneity in monetary unions. Using a unique micro-level dataset, we show that market finance premia, measured with corporate bond spreads, are remarkably similar in both the euro area and the US in terms of how little they depend on the issuer’s state or country of origin. In neither monetary union is the transmission of monetary policy to corporate bond rates differentiated as a function of the state or country of issuer. Unconditionally, the state or country of origin of the bond issuers explains very little of the variance among corporate bond spreads, in stark contrast to bank loan spreads that are determined at the country level for the same sample of bond-issuing firms. The euro area corporate bond market is as integrated as the US one, contrary to conventional beliefs. The marked difference between country influences on bank loan and corporate debt spreads is not due to selection effects in bond issuing firms but owes directly to the nature of market finance.

title: "Fanomenon": K-pop Industry Meets Competition?

detail.title: "Fanomenon": K-pop Industry Meets Competition?
detail.abstract: Recently, the four largest K-pop labels-HYBE, SM Entertainment, YG Entertainment, and JYP Entertainment-have proposed establishing a joint venture to create a Coachellastyle global K-pop festival, tentatively named "Fanomenon". This initiative is best understood against the backdrop of recent efforts by the Korean government to position Kpop as a strategic "core industry of the Korean economy." As the Korean government's industrial policy ambitions, including in the cultural sector, become increasingly explicit, this article, from a competition law expert's perspective, briefly sketches the competition concerns that may arise from this initiative, such as the possibility of an unduly broad market definition, the risk that the JV may serve as a hub for coordination, discriminatory foreclosure concerns affecting artists outside the four labels, and the broader concern that competition policy may once again be subordinated to industrial policy. Although it is too early to draw firm conclusions from the Fanomenon initiative, the paper nonetheless emphasizes the importance of preserving the competition authority's independent judgment, regardless of how the initiative ultimately develops.

title: Cognitive Liberty and Intellectual Property Rights: Who Owns the Output of a Neuralinked Mind?
affiliations: IILM UNIVERSITY

detail.title: Cognitive Liberty and Intellectual Property Rights: Who Owns the Output of a Neuralinked Mind?
detail.abstract:
Brain-computer interfaces have transitioned from speculative neuroscience into a tangible commercial product, with companies such as Neuralink demonstrating successful human implants since early 2024. These Devices Translate Raw Neural Signals into Digital commands,enabling paralysed individuals to operate computers, robotic arms, and communication software through thought alone. Yet this technological leap exposes a serious gap in intellectual property Jurisprudence: When a human mind collaborates with a Neural interface and its underlying algorithms to produce a creative work(a melody, a poem,a design), who holds authorship? This question is real and pressing, cutting across Copyright doctrine, patent law, cognitive liberty, and the emerging field of neuron rights. 

The present study undertakes a doctrinal and comparative analysis of the authorship problem that brain-computer interfaces create for intellectual property law. It examines how existing frameworks in the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and India grapple with the requirement of human authorship, tracing the trajectory from traditional copyright principles through landmark rulings such as Thaler v. Perlmutter and Naruto v. Slater. The paper then develops the concept of Joint authorship between the human mind and a Neural interface, arguing that neither the classical sole-author model nor the current artificial intelligence exclusion adequately captures the hybrid creative process that brain-computer interfaces facilitate. Drawing on the emerging discourse around Cognitive Liberty and neurorights, including Chile's pioneering 2021 constitutional amendment, the paper proposes a tiered authorship framework that allocates rights based on the degree of neural intentionality and algorithmic contribution. It concludes with specific Legislative Recommendations for national and international Bodies, urging that intellectual property reform keep pace with the neurotechnological revolution before commercial interest outstrips legal protections for the Human Mind.

title: Risk, Uncertainty, and the Probability of Missing a Target Return

detail.title: Risk, Uncertainty, and the Probability of Missing a Target Return
detail.abstract: Target return mandates such as "CPI +3%" are widely marketed, yet the standard mean-variance framework cannot assess the probability of achieving them. Multi-period compound returns are right-skewed, subject to volatility drag and sensitive to estimation uncertainty. This paper develops a lognormal framework for computing the probability of missing a target return over any horizon. The paper's principal contribution is a closed-form expression for the optimal investment horizon that minimises the probability of missing a target: H*=Δ/(3Ω) where Δ=μ-Rtarget is the return advantage and Ω=σ²/(2T) is the uncertainty drag rate. This U-shaped relationship reveals that even with an expected return advantage, estimation uncertainty eventually overwhelms its benefit. The probability of missing a target crosses 50% at exactly three times the optimal horizon.

title: Synthetic Kaleidic Media: AI, Interpretation, and Expectation Formation Under Radical Uncertainty

detail.title: Synthetic Kaleidic Media: AI, Interpretation, and Expectation Formation Under Radical Uncertainty
detail.abstract: This article develops an Austrian theory of synthetic kaleidic media. Starting from Knightian uncertainty, Shackleian imagination, Lachmannian kaleidics, Hayekian knowledge problems, and interpretive Austrian economics, it argues that media systems are not neutral channels for economic information but institutions of expectation formation. Media is always already kaleidic: it selects, arranges, and recombines the symbolic materials through which actors imagine futures and coordinate plans under uncertainty. AI and synthetic media do not create this condition, but transform it by lowering the cost of plausible symbolic production and embedding model-mediated interpretation into search, writing, analysis, advice, and decision. The article introduces symbolic calculation, symbolic convertibility, and action frames to explain how AI outputs enter plans: model-shaped salience affects actors' judgments of what is plausible, legitimate, risky, sayable, and actionable, and those judgments feed into plan revision and institutional feedback. The article connects this mechanism to narrative regimes, big players, entangled political economy, and a layered knowledge-attention-meaningexpectation commons. It concludes that the relevant institutional problem is not simply misinformation or AI safety in isolation, but comparative analysis of arrangements that preserve discovery, pluralism, contestability, and correction in synthetic kaleidic media environments.

title: Upgrading Housing – The Potential and Limits of Borrower-Based Measures

detail.title: Upgrading Housing – The Potential and Limits of Borrower-Based Measures
detail.abstract: Upgrading Europe's housing stock is essential to meeting EU climate goals, but borrower-based measures (BBMs) designed to protect financial stability can sometimes unintentionally restrict access to finance for housing upgrade projects. Drawing on experiences from Slovakia, Latvia, and Hungary, this brief examines how well-calibrated BBM easing can potentially expand lending for housing upgrades without undermining financial stability. Survey evidence from these countries shows that targeted easings pose minimal risk to financial stability but have had a limited impact on loan volumes. We explain this low uptake by the fact that BBM easings affect only a narrow group of borrowers and provide no direct financial incentive for renovations. To achieve meaningful impact, we suggest pairing BBM adjustments with fiscal measures, simplified administrative processes, and public awareness campaigns.

detail.abstract:
Background: The dynamics of multimorbidity accumulation across the life course are still incompletely understood. In particular, it is uncertain whether the rate of multimorbidity accumulation depends on the age at onset of the first chronic condition. 

Methods: We investigated these dynamics using longitudinal data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe and the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, including  25,058 individuals aged 50–70 years at baseline who were followed for up to 16 years. Multimorbidity was operationalized as count of ten major chronic conditions. 

Findings; Age was a strong and consistent predictor of increasing disease count over time, independent of the age at study entry. Individuals with less than four diseases at baseline showed steeper increases in multimorbidity than those with four or more baseline diseases, likely due to ceiling effect. Participants who developed their first disease at older ages experienced a more rapid subsequent accumulation of additional conditions compared with those whose first disease occurred earlier in life. The effect of age on disease accumulation was consistent across different stages of multimorbidity progression. Finally, the age at onset of the first disease was centred at approximately 73 years and showed little variation across disease types, suggesting no systematic tendency for specific conditions to be diagnosed earlier than others. 

Interpretation: Aging plays a central role in shaping multimorbidity trajectories and later onset of the first chronic disease may signal reduced physiological resilience and increased susceptibility to further disease accumulation.

detail.abstract: We test whether Weibull Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) survival models can replace the fixed aggregation window in HMM-based regime-aware execution with a per-instance prediction of remaining bearish regime duration. Fitting models to 54 bearish regime instances across eight asset classes (2020-2024), we find the extension fails on three structural grounds. First, concordance indices of 0.20-0.39 confirm that HMM-derived covariates, posterior entropy and stay probability at regime start, carry no duration-predictive information under parametric AFT models. Second, a without-replacement subsampling simulation shows Cindex remains flat at approximately 0.48 from n = 4 to n = 45 training instances, ruling out data quantity as the cause. Third, Weibull shape parameters below 1.0 in every asset class produce decreasing-hazard distributions whose mean durations structurally exceed the window cap, collapsing 60-89% of predictions to boundary values regardless of covariate values. There are no genuine adaptive wins over the fixed W = 10 baseline established in prior work. Together, Papers I-III characterize the limits of HMM-based regime awareness in execution: regime signals require multi-day aggregation (Paper II), learned policies cannot exploit them reliably (Paper I), and adaptive window calibration via parametric survival models is not achievable with HMM posteriors as duration predictors (Paper III).

title: Import Dependence and Industrial Adaptation: Strategic Responses of the Philippines to China's Manufacturing Dominance
