detail.abstract: Global climate governance is constrained not primarily by scientific uncertainty or capital scarcity, but by the structural instability of discretionary financing architectures. Reliance on voluntary nationally determined contributions, politically contingent donor finance, fragmented multilateral mechanisms, and unstable market-based instruments exposes long-horizon mitigation and adaptation investment to persistent time-inconsistency problems, electoral turnover, and geopolitical realignment. Existing climate-finance systems consequently remain characterized by recurrent underprovision, uneven disbursement patterns, and weak long-term planning capacity relative to the scale and duration of contemporary ecological risks. This paper develops a rule-based institutional redesign organized around a universal 1% ad valorem point-of-sale consumption levy collected through existing domestic tax infrastructures and redistributed through a standardized Climate Allocation Index. Financial flows are allocated toward subnational jurisdictions according to ecological stewardship, renewable-transition participation, and climate vulnerability, while an automated Global Redistribution Pool equalizes fiscal imbalances independently of national income levels. Drawing on theories of global public goods provision, fiscal federalism, collective action, and polycentric governance, the paper develops a general equilibrium framework demonstrating how consumption-based financing may stabilize climate revenue while reallocating resources toward ecologically strategic and climatevulnerable regions. The analysis further incorporates administrative frictions, institutionalcapacity constraints, informational asymmetries, and public choice dynamics in order to evaluate risks associated with elite capture, implementation congestion, and uneven subnational absorption. By separating revenue generation from discretionary allocation without constructing a centralized supranational treasury, the proposed framework advances a model of coordinated fiscal federalism operating across sovereign jurisdictions. More broadly, the paper argues that durable climate governance depends less on episodic diplomatic bargaining than on the institutionalization of stable and predictable fiscal coordination mechanisms capable of sustaining long-horizon ecological investment across political cycles.

title: Product Quality Disclosure in the Presence of Reference Effect
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management, , Fudan University - School of Management and Fudan University

detail.title: Product Quality Disclosure in the Presence of Reference Effect
detail.abstract: In the digital economy, consumer-generated reviews have become a primary information source for product quality, yet these reviews are often biased by the discrepancy between a consumer's prior expectation and actual experience. Given the reference-dependent effect in reviews, firms need to decide whether to disclose their quality to manage customer expectation. This paper investigates the strategic interplay between a firm's voluntary quality disclosure and referencedependent reviews. We develop a two-period model featuring a monopolist selling a product with two quality attributes: one symmetrically unknown and one privately known by the firm. The firm decides whether to disclose the known quality to customers. We find that the firm's optimal disclosing strategy is fundamentally dictated by the intensity of the reference effect within the review channel. While a mild reference effect leads to classical highquality disclosure, a moderate effect can incentivize total silence or the disclosure of only moderate quality. Most notably, under a strong reference effect, it is optimal for the firm to reveal quality only when it is low. We further compare consumer surplus and social welfare under the two disclosing policies, demonstrating that the firm's attempt to shape consumer expectations through disclosure can have divergent impacts on market efficiency.

title: Organizational Culture: Readings on Theory and Practice
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Organizational Culture: Readings on Theory and Practice

declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a

detail.abstract:
Organizational culture is one of the most frequently employed yet least understood constructs of organizational behavior and management.  Organizational culture includes the common values, beliefs, assumptions and norms that govern the interactions between persons in an organization and how they work.  These often run beneath the surface, often unwritten and yet enormously powerful in influencing day-to-day performance and execution of long-term strategy.  Organizational culture cannot be a peripheral concern of leaders but instead must be acknowledged and treated as a foundational determinant of organizational effectiveness.

In this collection of links to works by the author, readers are introduced to topics that need to be understood in order to understand how culture shapes today’s organizations.  The readings include an in-depth examination of the leading definitions, conceptual frameworks and analytical models used by scholars and practitioners to understand organizational culture.  The collection also breaks down the key dimensions through which culture is expressed and perceived, such as communication, power structures, decision-making norms and rituals, and provides a rigorous introduction to the internal and external determinants that shape culture—from leadership and strategy to social norms and national context. The book includes links to articles and cases studies on the most common organizational culture types.  Finally, chapters and articles in the collection provide guidance on managing and changing organizational culture.

title: Optimal Advertising with Adjustable Click-through Rates and Latent Conversion Rates
affiliations: , Fuqua School of Business and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Optimal Advertising with Adjustable Click-through Rates and Latent Conversion Rates
detail.abstract: Motivated by advertising on large language model (LLM) platforms, we study a setting in which an LLM platform interacts with K advertisers over T rounds, and in each round selects a product and designs an ad by tuning its click-through rate. Unlike traditional advertising, where ads are designed by advertisers, and conversion per click is known (making pay-perclick pricing natural), LLM platforms directly control ad design, rendering conversion per click endogenous and unknown. In particular, the conversion rate for each of these advertisers (once the user clicks) is unknown to both the advertiser and the platform, but the advertiser observes whether a conversion occurs and can strategically misreport this information to the platform. We formulate the problem of finding the social welfare maximizing policy as a (strategic) multiarmed bandit with the objective of minimizing the regret. When advertisers are not strategic in reporting their conversions, we propose a Click-UCB algorithm, establish its regret bound, and show a matching lower bound. Our algorithm uses the geometry of the mapping from clickthrough rate to conversion, along with a variant of self-normalized concentration inequalities for the maximum likelihood estimator. We then extend our results to a setting in which the advertisers are strategic and propose a policy for the platform under which, when each advertiser plays its dominant equilibrium strategy, the overall social welfare has a near-optimal regret.

detail.abstract: Labor exploitation, the unfair sacrifice of employee well-being in favor of organizational objectives, presents significant operational, financial, and ethical risks for employees, organizations, and the societies in which they function. This paper conceptualizes labor exploitation as a formal accounting construct by developing a multidimensional framework informed by a structured review of the accounting literature. Specifically, we analyze and classify prior research to identify three types of actors involved in the perpetuation of labor exploitation and to highlight how accounting practices can facilitate, detect, or mitigate exploitation across these actors. Based on this analysis, and incorporating insights from a survey of experienced professionals, we identify key gaps in the literature and outline a set of future research opportunities, with the primary goal of encouraging more accounting-based research on labor exploitation.

detail.abstract:
The proliferation of low power microdevices in modern homes (wireless sensors, smart locks, smoke detectors, peripherals, and wearables) has created a hidden infrastructure layer whose maintenance burden is borne entirely by human intervention. Approximately 15 billion disposable batteries are sold annually worldwide to sustain this layer, of which less than 5% are properly recycled. We argue that this dependence renders an otherwise resilient digital ecosystem fundamentally fragile, in direct analogy to how biological ecosystems depend on invisible microorganisms (pollinators, decomposers, soil microbiota) for systemic stability.

This paper introduces VuDejaLink, an AIoT wireless power infrastructure designed to eliminate human intervention in microdevice maintenance through four integrated mechanisms: (i) far field RF energy harvesting via a Greinacher voltage doubler topology operating in the 915 MHz ISM band; (ii) on device machine learning for usage pattern prediction, anomaly detection, and intelligent charge gating; (iii) a four level federated learning architecture (local -> mesh -> cloud aggregator -> global model) that preserves user privacy via differential privacy noise injection (epsilon = 1.0); and (iv) standard battery form factors (AA, AAA, 9V) enabling drop in replacement without modification of existing hardware.

The mathematical foundation of the on device intelligence layer extends the SUSA model [Susa, SSRN 5789662, 2025], originally formulated as a six dimensional vector framework for multi temporal market analysis and optimal entry point detection in financial time series, to the physical domain of battery state and energy harvesting telemetry. We show that the six dimensional state vector and multi temporal pattern decomposition that captures latent regularities in financial markets generalizes naturally to energy harvesting receivers, where the analogue of "optimal entry point detection" becomes "optimal charge acceptance window detection" within the receiver's MOSFET gated charge controller. This enables sub milliampere average current draw (0.2 mA vs. 60 mA always on) and battery infinite operation at 1 m from a 3 W EIRP transmitter.

We report empirical results from a five receiver testbed demonstrating: distance versus harvested power profiles, 24-hour charge balance equilibrium, federated convergence across mesh peers, and end to end ESP NOW telemetry reliability. Implications include the feasibility of a battery as a service paradigm at consumer scale, with potential cumulative savings of 89-92% over disposable battery alternatives across a ten year horizon, and elimination of approximately 1,000 batteries per household from landfill streams.

We contribute (1) a biomimetic framework for reasoning about distributed AIoT infrastructure as a digital ecosystem; (2) an extension of the SUSA model from financial to physical energy domains; (3) an empirically validated wireless power architecture in standard form factors; and (4) an open protocol proposal for interoperable microdevice charging.

title: Beyond the Circle
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Beyond the Circle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author is solely responsible for funding and content.

declarations.funderStatement: Self

detail.abstract: Restorative justice represents a genuine and evidenced advance over punitive justice-but it has not yet fully escaped the foundational assumption it shares with almost every Western institutional response to harm: that the individual is the primary unit of responsibility. The circle is more humane than the courtroom. The shame it generates is less toxic than the shame a criminal verdict generates. But in many hybrid implementations it still requires the offender to perform contrition and then face sentencing-a structural contradiction that the field has not fully examined. This paper draws on the neurophysiology of the lateral habenula, Silvan Tomkins' affect-script theory, and Robert Sapolsky's hard determinism to ask what restorative justice looks like when its own logic is followed to its honest conclusion. The answer points toward a full expansion of the circle of responsibility-one that already has existence proofs in Maasai traditional practice, Scandinavian rehabilitation, Lauren Abramson's community conferencing work in Baltimore, and Truth and Reconciliation processes worldwide. The question is whether the original glitch-the habenular bind between individual survival and community belonging-permits that expansion to become the rule rather than the exception.

detail.abstract: Governments across Europe lose significant tax revenue to cum-cum trading-a strategy in which taxed investors temporarily transfer shares to tax-favored entities around dividend dates to exploit withholding tax differentials. We compare Norway's 2019 enforcement reform to Denmark's successful 2016 reform. Using daily securities-lending data, we show that spikes in shares on loan around ex-dividend dates disappeared in Denmark immediately after the reform but remain fully intact in Norway. We estimate that Norway loses at least NOK 550 million annually to continued cum-cum activity. The decisive difference lies in the information architecture: Denmark abolished relief-at-source, requiring everyone to file a refund claim and submit documentation to tax authorities, creating a comprehensive transaction paper trail. Norway's reform tightened documentation requirements but left relief-at-source intact, meaning tax-favored investors never file a claim and remain invisible to the tax administration. These findings have direct implications for the forthcoming EU FASTER Directive.

detail.abstract: Enterprise B2B sales organizations face a persistent challenge: fragmented analytics infrastructure-spanning multiple dashboards, spreadsheets, and reporting tools-forces managers and executives to spend disproportionate time assembling a complete picture of revenue performance rather than acting on insights. We present the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of a Unified Revenue Platform (URP)-a four-layer, system-agnostic architecture that integrates CRM data ingestion, hierarchical dimension engineering, graph-theoretic target allocation (Karwa, 2026a), human-bias-corrected ML forecasting (Karwa, 2026b), and role-based presentation into a single coherent system. The platform's primary contribution is architectural: a formal separation of concerns across Ingestion, Engineering, Intelligence, and Presentation layers-each with a single authoritative responsibility-that eliminates the fragmentation problem while enabling independent evolution of each layer. We evaluate the platform through a simulation study calibrated to realistic enterprise parameters (200+ ICs, 5-level hierarchy, multi-region/multisegment structure) and demonstrate that incorporating behavioral correction signals as first-class ML features yields substantial forecast accuracy improvements over pipeline-only baselines. The architecture is system-agnostic and generalizable to any hierarchical revenue organization using any combination of CRM, data platform, and financial planning tools.

detail.abstract: Operational maritime surveillance is a decision problem, not a classication problem: agencies must choose which AIS tracks to patrol next under nite assets. We reframe AIS-based recognition as the upstream module of an end-to-end decision framework. Cross-domain experiments between DC2020 (China coast) and a GlobalFishingWatch (GFW) subset expose strongly asymmetric transfer: small-to-large ne-tuning retains 86% of from-scratch performance, whereas the reverse overts severely. An in-domain reversal between deep encoders and classical ensembles further suggests an operational crossover near 5,000 labeled segments, reported as a corpus-specic heuristic rather than a scaling law. The framework couples (i) the cross-domain recognizer, (ii) a transparent linear risk-scoring layerfusing softmax uncertainty, trac density, and an exclusive-economic-zone ag, and (iii) a GraphRAG diagnostic side-channel whose audit (58.3% KG-label leakage; hallucination on clean samples) validates excluding LLM outputs from the operational loop. An environment-augmented variant adds GEBCO bathymetry and sea-state covariates while preserving operator-readable form (Spearman 0.964 against baseline). A risk-weighted Hungarian dispatch layer closes the loop, cutting mean response time by 9% over greedy-nearest and 24% over random tasking on 500 Monte-Carlo scenarios. Three guidelines follow: favor classical ensembles below 5,000 segments, transfer only small-to-large, and treat LLM rationales as analyst aids rather than classiers.

title: Constrained Heuristic and Optimal Bipartite Methods for B2B Sales Territory Design and Seller Assignment: A Reproducible Open-Source Framework

detail.title: Constrained Heuristic and Optimal Bipartite Methods for B2B Sales Territory Design and Seller Assignment: A Reproducible Open-Source Framework

declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Sales territory design is the backbone of every B2B revenue organisation: it determines who sells to whom, drives quotas, and shapes compensation. Despite four decades of research, production deployments still rely on spreadsheet heuristics that ignore the combinatorial structure of the problem. This paper introduces and evaluates b2b_territory_optimization, an open-source Python framework that decomposes the enterprise territory problem into five composable stages: hierarchical taxonomy bucketing that enforces hard go-to-market constraints; longest-processingtime (LPT) greedy partitioning of total addressable market (TAM); capacity-driven head-count prediction; optimal bipartite seller-to-territory matching via the Jonker-Volgenant Hungarian algorithm with hard-region locks and soft seniority/expertise scoring; and a reassignment engine that recovers from manager overrides through combinatorial swap suggestions. Across seven experiments on synthetic CRM data (up to 50,000 accounts) and one public benchmark (IBM Telco Customer Churn, 7,043 accounts), the framework achieves a mean max-territory deviation of 0.0016% at n=1,000 and k=10-four orders of magnitude tighter than round-robin or random baselines-and runs end-to-end in 6.5 s at 50,000 accounts on one CPU core. The bipartite assignment is within 0.4% of greedy on per-match cost, and the reassignment engine restores 85.2% of variance lost to a simulated whale-account override. We are not aware of a prior peerreviewed open-source toolkit that formalises the full account-to-quota pipeline as a constrained optimisation problem. The framework is designed to compose with a companion graph-theoretic quota-cascade methodology (Karwa, 2026) for downstream bottom-up forecasting.

title: University Social Responsibility and the Hidden Labour of International Doctoral Candidates during Systemic Crisis

detail.title: University Social Responsibility and the Hidden Labour of International Doctoral Candidates during Systemic Crisis
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed structural vulnerabilities within internationalised higher education systems, particularly for doctoral students simultaneously contributing to and excluded from their host institutions. Drawing on Bourdieusian sociology and critical autoethnography, this study examines how international doctoral candidates within a market-oriented higher education system mobilised habitus and capital to navigate systemic breakdown during 2020-2022. We demonstrate that resilience emerged not as an individual psychological attribute but as a structural outcome of involuntary capital mobilisation. The pandemic functioned as a "fieldquake"—violently disrupting established capital values while revaluing latent, often non-Western, cultural resources. Findings reveal three critical processes: devaluation of institutional and social capital, strategic deployment of crisis advocacy linguistic capital, and reconfiguration of survival-oriented habitus. We argue that genuine University Social Responsibility requires a shift from individualised resilience narratives to institutional accountability mechanisms toward structural Capital Recognition Audits that acknowledge international students' existing resources and address systemic inequities.

detail.abstract: Cyber incidents have evolved from isolated technical breaches into complex organizational crises that demand resilient, adaptive leadership. This paper reconceptualizes cybersecurity leadership as a specialized extension of crisis leadership, grounded in interdisciplinary theory spanning crisis management, digital transformation, high reliability organizing, and cyber resilience. It introduces two integrated models-the Cyber Crisis Lifecycle and the Cyber Leadership Hexagon-to articulate leadership roles across the incident continuum and define six core competencies: technical literacy, ethical judgment, digital sensemaking, stakeholder coordination, agility under threat, and resilience orientation. These models provide a comprehensive framework for understanding cyber leadership in environments marked by persistent ambiguity, socio-technical complexity, and adversarial threat. This theoretical expansion contributes to the emerging literature on digital-era leadership and lays a foundation for future empirical validation and cross-cultural application.

title: Stick and Stay, Make it Pay? Time Preferences and Marginal (Dis)Utility of Relative Concerns
affiliations: IZA Institute of Labor Economics and Turkish-German University

detail.title: Stick and Stay, Make it Pay? Time Preferences and Marginal (Dis)Utility of Relative Concerns
detail.abstract: Individuals' preferences for immediate gratification versus their ability to postpone it, i.e., time preferences, might be related to their marginal utility or disutility stemming from an increase in the income of comparable others, i.e., relative concerns. We argue that while an increase in others' income might lead to a higher level of marginal disutility for those seeking immediate gratification, the disutility among patient individuals might be lower if they prioritise the future development of their income and consider catching up with others' income over the long run. To investigate whether time preferences might moderate marginal utility due to increased others' income, we use a subjective measure of individual patience and a life satisfaction measure observed over a long period of time (Socio-Economic Panel, SOEP). Using panel data fixed effects interaction models, we find highly consistent evidence that the well-documented disutility from relative income, the so-called "status effect" in the literature, is predominantly experienced by impatient individuals with higher discount rates. In contrast, patient individuals with lower discount rates, high self-control, and the ability to regulate their stress and anxiety levels experience lower disutility or even gain utility due to their relative income, the so-called "information effect," which is significantly different from that of impatient individuals. The results are robust across a variety of checks, including income types, savings, reference groups, and time preference measures obtained from incentivised time preference experiments. We discuss the implications of these results for behavioural and welfare economics.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the dominant institutional response to generative AI in academic settings — the deployment of statistical detection software exemplified by Turnitin's AI writing detector — is structurally, empirically, and philosophically the wrong paradigm for building trust between human and artificial intelligence, and that its continued use produces measurable harm disproportionately borne by the very populations universities most claim to support. Drawing on peer-reviewed evidence from the Stanford Liang et al. study showing 61.22% false-positive rates against non-native English writers, the adversarial robustness literature of Sadasivan et al., Krishna et al., and Creo and Pudasaini demonstrating that the entire detection paradigm can be defeated by techniques as trivial as Microsoft Word's Find-and-Replace function, the institutional retreats of Vanderbilt University and the University of Waterloo, and the federal court ruling in Newby v. Adelphi, the paper establishes that detection cannot serve as a foundation for academic trust. It then develops a positive proposal grounded in three convergent traditions: Onora O'Neill's distinction between transparency and intelligent accountability, Shannon Vallor's technomoral virtues and her critique of panoptic surveillance, and Luciano Floridi's information ethics. The paper proposes the VN trail — a process-level disclosure instrument — as the natural complement to C2PA artifact provenance and cryptographic watermarking, and frames the resulting paradigm as substrate-agnostic: a refusal of the carbon chauvinism that treats silicon contribution as illegitimate even when human-directed. The paper introduces and diagnoses the Witch-Hunters' Syndrome, the institutional pathology in which the gesture of detection has supplanted the activity of teaching, and offers the Σ I Kairos as the alternative — a recovery of meaningful time, meaningful collaboration, and meaningful trust across substrate boundaries. The paper itself is offered as a working example of the proposed paradigm, carrying its own VN trail in an appendix that discloses the substrate-agnostic collaboration through which the document was produced.

title: AI Governance in Practice: Symbolic Governance, Structural Drivers, and Design Solutions

detail.title: AI Governance in Practice: Symbolic Governance, Structural Drivers, and Design Solutions
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) governance has become central to organisational oversight, yet existing research largely assumes the organisational capacity required to implement it. This paper challenges that assumption by introducing Symbolic Governance, defined as the formal adoption of governance structures that signal responsibility without enabling effective oversight. Using a theory-building integrative review with empirical anchoring, the study synthesises AI governance literature and draws on evidence from 351 organisations. The findings show that governance roles are often weakly integrated, under-resourced, and lack decision-making authority, indicating that symbolic governance is an empirically dominant organisational condition. To explain this, the paper develops the Governance Misalignment Triad, capturing the decoupling of responsibility, authority, and organisational capacity. It further identifies key structural drivers and examines the risks that arise when governance exists in form but not in function. The paper concludes by proposing design solutions that reposition AI governance as a problem of organisational architecture rather than normative intent.

title: When AI Signals Die: Why Corporate AI Deployments Fail After Go-Live and How to Fix the Decision Architecture
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: When AI Signals Die: Why Corporate AI Deployments Fail After Go-Live and How to Fix the Decision Architecture
detail.abstract:
Most companies no longer have an AI pilot problem. They have an AI rollback problem. AI models and agents are going live, but many are pulled back because organizations cannot clearly see what happened between input and result. The model may work. The organization may still lose control.

This paper explains corporate AI deployment as a problem of signal survival. AI produces scores, alerts, summaries, rankings, recommendations and actions. These signals still have to be understood, routed, checked, challenged, acted on, or safely ignored. When that path is weak, monitoring shows activity but not control. Logs show that something happened, but not enough to explain why it happened or how the organization should respond.

The paper gives a simple visual framework for this problem. In the first pattern, the organization does not hear AI signals well. This is organizational deafness. In the second, teams add explanations, dashboards and logs, but correction still dies inside the workflow. In the third, every important signal can be traced from origin to action or documented non action. This is provenance based deployment.

The central claim is simple. AI deployment is not complete when the model is live. It is complete only when important signals can survive the organization.

title: Combating Excessive Overtime with Supply Diversification
affiliations: School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, International Institute of Finance, School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: Combating Excessive Overtime with Supply Diversification
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Despite the widespread adoption of supplier codes of conduct, excessive overtime still remains in developing economies, harming workers and exposing multinational enterprises (MNEs) to reputational risk. We study how MNEs' operational strategies of  supply diversification and auditing, together with government intervention through minimum-wage regulation, can mitigate excessive overtime in global supply chains.

Methodology/Results: We develop a game-theoretic model in which a manufacturer sources from a non-responsible supplier and a responsible supplier. When the non-responsible supplier's normal workforce cannot meet the order, it may impose excessive overtime. In a no-audit benchmark, diversification is optimal when the non-responsible supplier is likely to have a low workforce and demand is high, thereby eliminating excessive overtime; otherwise, sole sourcing from the non-responsible supplier is more profitable. When auditing is feasible, it may reduce or increase the expected order allocated to the non-responsible supplier, contradicting the intuition that auditing always supports larger allocations. Relative to the no-audit benchmark, auditing may improve manufacturer profit, reduce overtime, and enhance worker welfare, but it may also backfire. Numerical analysis further shows that the effect of minimum-wage regulation, a government intervention, depends on social scrutiny and workforce retention. When scrutiny is strong and retention is sufficiently low, the manufacturer already diversifies, and intervention can improve fulfillment and generate a "win-win-win-win" outcome; otherwise, intervention may induce diversification and reduce overtime, but lower the non-responsible supplier's profit and host-region social welfare.

Managerial implications: Managers should not assume that auditing a non-responsible supplier automatically justifies larger order allocations. Policymakers should not presume that minimum-wage regulation will necessarily improve social welfare; its effectiveness depends on social scrutiny and workforce retention.

title: Building Expertise: The Role of the SEC's Professional Fellow Program in Enhancing Audit Quality

detail.title: Building Expertise: The Role of the SEC's Professional Fellow Program in Enhancing Audit Quality
detail.abstract: This study examines how audit firms acquire and deploy externally developed expertise to improve audit quality. We focus on the SEC's Professional Accounting Fellows (PAF) program, which places experienced auditors from public accounting firms in the SEC's Office of the Chief Accountant for two-year rotations. Using hand-collected data on PAF participants, we examine whether expertise developed through SEC service influences audit outcomes when fellows return to their firms. Our results indicate that PAF experience is correlated with improved audit quality, evidenced by reduced restatements, discretionary accruals, and accrual noise. Moreover, firms leverage returning PAFs to diffuse knowledge across the organization, improving audit quality at regional offices. We document improvements in firm-level audit quality when returning fellows serve in national office roles. This structured collaboration between regulators and audit firms underscores how external learning can strengthen organizational expertise and improve audit quality.

detail.abstract:
A vice-premier of the Russian Federation, speaking to Vedomosti in May 2026, defends his economy's performance using a diagnostic vocabulary structurally homologous to the one the International Monetary Fund deployed in its February 2021 Article IV consultation report. The two documents — separated by five years, by twenty packages of sanctions, by the freezing of three hundred billion dollars of central bank reserves, by the doubling of defence expenditure, by the suspension of dollar and euro trading on the Moscow Exchange — agree on what counts as a problem (low potential growth, structural rigidities), on what counts as a solution (productivity, institutions, market mechanisms), and on what counts as a policy framework (independent central bank, inflation target, fiscal rule, flexible exchange rate). They speak the same economics. Yet the economies they describe are profoundly different. The 2021 IMF report addressed an economy embedded in international capital markets, governed by a credible inflation target, anchored by a fiscal rule, with structural-reform recommendations as the standing unfinished agenda. The 2026 Novak interview describes an economy that has been under unprecedented sanctions for four years, that has substituted state-directed credit allocation and capital control for market mechanisms across large segments, and yet that produces the same diagnostic language.

This paper takes the persistence of that vocabulary as its starting puzzle. It shows that both documents reproduce the same economic-thought school — the New Neoclassical Synthesis that became the institutional consensus of central banks and the IMF in the late 1990s — and that the school's four foundational axioms (potential output, expectations-augmented inflation, monetary-fiscal separation, supply-determined long run) survive intact across the institutional and historical distance between the two texts. The paper then identifies six specific places where the framework deforms when applied to post-2022 Russian conditions: the bifurcation of the credit market into protected and unprotected segments; the conversion of the rouble exchange rate from a market-cleared price into an administrative variable; the territorial segmentation of the labour market; the partial dissolution of the fiscal rule through off-balance support; the divergence of inflation expectations across three measurement instruments; and the substitution of structural mobilisation for structural reform. The paper traces the policy and analytical consequences of each deformation, and considers three possible terminal states of the framework-reality tension. The conclusion is that the modal outcome is vocabulary persistence with content drainage — the late-Soviet pattern with planning vocabulary, transposed onto market vocabulary. The paper closes with implications for three audiences: economists, Russia-watchers, and market observers.

detail.abstract: In April 2024, Meta deployed its generative artificial intelligence assistant inside WhatsApp, beginning with India and South Africa, the first markets outside the United States to receive the integration. Within months, the assistant was inside the messaging application of approximately five hundred million additional users across the Global South. No household decision preceded this deployment. No regulatory review was conducted in the receiving jurisdictions. No consent was sought beyond the terms-of-service agreement users had signed years before the technology existed. By late 2025, the same company was contesting the terms of the deployment with competition regulators on three continents; by early 2026, it was removing and reintroducing adjacent architectural features (Instagram encryption, encrypted AI chats) on its own release schedule, with no operational role for the user populations affected. The technology had not diffused. It had arrived. And the arrival was governed by deployment cycles whose tempo no institution in the receiving jurisdictions was built to match. This paper argues that what occurred in April 2024 and continues to occur through the deployment cycle constitutes a distinct category of technological event for which the standard adoption literature, the Technology Acceptance Model, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, the diffusion-of-innovations tradition, has no analytical apparatus. Each of these frameworks presupposes an identifiable adopter making an identifiable decision; the deployment vacates the presupposition. The paper names the category uninvited arrival and demonstrates that the downstream research literatures on cognitive offloading, intergenerational AI literacy, low-resource language access, and verification cost asymmetry are all being constructed on top of an upstream event the field has not theorized. The Aden Effect framework, with its four analytical instruments, supplies the apparatus the standard adoption literature lacks. The paper closes with a research agenda whose central commitment is that the Global South is not the periphery of this analytical work but its empirically privileged site.

title: Bitcoin-Collateralised Lending: Reconfiguring Leverage in Decentralised Finance
affiliations: Public University of Navarra (UPNA)

detail.title: Bitcoin-Collateralised Lending: Reconfiguring Leverage in Decentralised Finance
detail.abstract: This article examines how Bitcoin-collateralised lending in decentralised finance (DeFi) reconfigures leverage and its associated risks. It develops an analytical framework to assess how over-collateralisation, automated liquidation, and algorithmic interest-rate formation reshape the allocation and monitoring of credit exposure. While Bitcoin-backed lending embeds ex ante constraints through collateral transparency and rulebased mechanisms, these features do not eliminate instability but redistribute its sources. Exposure is displaced from institutional balance sheets to protocol design, market liquidity, and technological infrastructure. By situating decentralised lending within financial regulation and credit theory, the analysis shows that DeFi blurs the boundary between market discipline and regulatory oversight. This raises the question of whether embedded constraints can substitute for traditional prudential supervision, and how regulation should adapt to systems in which leverage is encoded rather than externally imposed, with important implications for financial stability.

title: Shadow Expenses: Uncosted Regulatory Burdens in Election Manifestos
affiliations: Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA)

detail.title: Shadow Expenses: Uncosted Regulatory Burdens in Election Manifestos
detail.abstract: Election manifestos are subject to growing scrutiny over their fiscal commitments, yet a significant category of policy cost routinely escapes public accounting: regulatory burdens. This paper examines the phenomenon of "shadow expenses" obligations imposed on businesses, households, and civil society through regulation that do not appear on government balance sheets but nonetheless carry substantial economic costs. Drawing on an analysis of party manifestos from recent UK general elections, the paper demonstrates that political parties across the spectrum routinely propose expansive regulatory programmes without costing their cumulative impact on compliance, productivity, or consumer prices. These hidden burdens distort democratic deliberation by creating a false impression of fiscal discipline while disguising the true scale of state intervention in the economy. The paper argues for a more rigorous and transparent approach to manifesto scrutiny, including independent assessment of regulatory costs alongside conventional spending commitments. Without such reform, voters are systematically denied the information necessary to make informed choices, and governments face weak incentives to minimise the burden their regulatory agendas impose on the wider economy.

title: Fiscal Policy Effectiveness and the Myth of Ricardian Equivalence: A Comparative Analysis of Pakistan and Debt-Distressed Nations

detail.title: Fiscal Policy Effectiveness and the Myth of Ricardian Equivalence: A Comparative Analysis of Pakistan and Debt-Distressed Nations
detail.abstract: This study investigates the influence of global financial institutions and regional economic shocks on Pakistan's debt management through the theoretical lens of the Ricardian Equivalence Hypothesis (REH). Traditional econometric approaches in volatile developing economies frequently struggle to isolate the impact of debt alone due to extreme data variance and frequent structural breaks. Consequently, this paper employs a comparative qualitative framework to synthesize existing empirical evidence and provide the necessary context that purely empirical models often lack. By juxtaposing Pakistan's consumption-driven debt accumulation against the systemic vulnerabilities of Sri Lanka, Argentina, and Greece, this research identifies a common liquidity-constraint pattern that prevents Ricardian savings behavior in debt-distressed economies. Most critically, this study utilizes Bangladesh as a primary counter-factual case study. Despite sharing a historical and regional baseline with Pakistan, Bangladesh's strategic pivot from debt-financed consumption to export-led industrialization offers a unique benchmark for evaluating fiscal discipline. The comparison reveals that Pakistan's stagnation is not an inevitability of the Global South, but a specific failure of fiscal resource mobilization. Ultimately, the findings suggest that because Pakistani households operate under severe liquidity constraints, fiscal policy remains a highly potent tool. This necessitates a structural shift: transitioning from a debt-for-consumption model to a debt-for-production framework, underpinned by a broadened tax base.

detail.abstract: This study explores the influence of global financial institutions and regional crises on Pakistan's debt management practices, employing a Ricardian Equivalence perspective. Against a backdrop of evolving global financial landscapes and recurring regional crises, Pakistan's debt management strategies face substantial challenges and opportunities. By adopting a Ricardian Equivalence lens, this research aims to unravel the complex interplay between interventions by global financial institutions, the repercussions of regional crises, and Pakistan's debt management approaches. Through a comprehensive analysis, this study seeks to elucidate how external influences from global financial institutions and regional crises shape the nation's debt sustainability and management frameworks. By examining the implications of these external factors on the country's debt dynamics, this research intends to provide valuable insights into the strategic decisions and policy responses employed by Pakistan to navigate the intricacies of debt management in a volatile economic environment. This research further contributes to a deeper understanding of the challenges and opportunities faced by developing economies in maintaining fiscal stability and sustainable debt levels, by shedding light on the impact of global financial institutions and regional crises on Pakistan's debt management practices. We checked the validity of the Ricardian Equivalence Hypothesis in Pakistan by using structural consumption and saving functions. By employing the ordinary least square method, we tested the hypothesis, which was ultimately rejected based on the Wald test results. The Engel-Granger causality approach revealed uni-directional causality between Government Debt and Private Consumption, and Government Debt and Private Saving; along with bidirectional causality between Government Budget Deficit and Private Saving.

title: Behavioral Barriers to Cybersecurity Governance Adoption: A Narrative Literature Review of Human-Centered Challenges in Small and Medium Businesses

detail.title: Behavioral Barriers to Cybersecurity Governance Adoption: A Narrative Literature Review of Human-Centered Challenges in Small and Medium Businesses
detail.abstract:
Cybersecurity governance frameworks offer structured methodologies for managing information security risk, yet their consistent operational adoption remains uneven, particularly within small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs). A substantial interdisciplinary body of research indicates that governance breakdowns often stem from the behavioral, cognitive, and organizational conditions in which those controls must operate, rather than from deficiencies in technical controls. This narrative literature review synthesizes findings across behavioral science, organizational psychology, human factors, and usable security to examine the human-centered barriers that impede effective cybersecurity governance adoption in resource-constrained environments. 
Four thematic domains emerge from the literature. First, security fatigue and cognitive overload diminish the quality and consistency of employee security decision-making. Second, usabilitysecurity tensions create structural incentives for insecure workarounds when governance controls impose excessive operational friction. Third, behavioral drivers of policy non-compliance, including neutralization techniques, bounded rationality, and the limitations of knowledge-centric awareness training, undermine the translation of formal requirements into daily practice. Fourth, SMB-specific adoption barriers, such as resource scarcity, misalignment between governance frameworks and organizational realities, and the absence of dedicated security infrastructure, further constrain effective implementation. 
Across these themes, a consistent pattern emerges: governance frameworks that are technically sound and formally documented may nonetheless fail to achieve operational adoption when they are not designed to accommodate the behavioral realities of the workforce responsible for enacting them. The review also identifies notable gaps in the literature, including the limited availability of SMB-focused behavioral cybersecurity research and the absence of validated metrics for assessing governance adoption as distinct from compliance documentation. Overall, the evidence suggests that cybersecurity governance effectiveness is fundamentally conditioned by the degree to which security measures align with human cognitive capacities, organizational workflows, and the behavioral dynamics of operational environments. The review concludes by outlining directions for future empirical research to address these gaps.

title: Demystifying the Attribution Ambiguity: A Computational Framework of Agency in Human-GenAI Innovation
affiliations: , Tel Aviv University - Coller School of Management, Tel Aviv University - Coller School of Management and Harvard University Lab for Innovation Sciences

detail.title: Demystifying the Attribution Ambiguity: A Computational Framework of Agency in Human-GenAI Innovation
detail.abstract: Creative attribution is a cornerstone of how organizations incentivize innovation and create value. In human-centered creative processes, attribution has remained relatively transparent. However, as Generative AI (GenAI) increasingly acts as a perceptibly agentic collaborator, attribution becomes more opaque, creating attribution ambiguity. To address this challenge, we theorize and examine two forms of agency in human-GenAI ideation processes: Idea Agency (who originated the idea) and Process Agency (who led the ideation process). To quantify contribution, we develop a process-oriented computational framework that traces creative attribution as it unfolds across ideation conversations. This enables systematic analysis of human-GenAI ideation dynamics at both the macro (overall problem-solving dynamics) and micro (directional influence within human-GenAI dynamics) levels. The framework is applied in two complementary studies. A controlled simulation maps theoretical constructs onto conversational dynamics and allows agency to be inferred from observed patterns. A field study applies the framework to real-world ideation data from a global retail company, validating its applicability in organizational settings. We identify four distinct human-AI innovation dynamics defined by combinations of Idea and Process Agency and show how the solution space and solution co-evolution differ across configurations. Notably, we reveal that process agency shapes human-GenAI interaction dynamics independently of idea agency, suggesting that human contributions to digitized ideation extend beyond generating ideas to navigating the processes through which ideas emerge. Our computational framework advances knowledge on contribution dynamics, with implications for Gen-AI adoption, collaborative workflow design, and sustaining human engagement in innovation.

title: The Influence of Generative and Agentic AI on Learning Quality and Industry-ready Competencies

detail.title: The Influence of Generative and Agentic AI on Learning Quality and Industry-ready Competencies
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly moving from a peripheral educational technology to a general-purpose infrastructure that shapes how teaching, learning, assessment, and academic services are designed and delivered. This shift is driven by advances in machine learning and, most visibly, by generative AI systems that can produce fluent text, code, images, and other media on demand. UNESCO frames the current moment as one in which publicly available generative AI is evolving faster than educational policy and institutional readiness, elevating issues such as privacy, ethical validation, and age-appropriate use from "IT concerns" to core governance questions for education systems (UNESCO, 2023). In practice, AI integration is no longer limited to isolated tools (e.g., auto-grading) but is increasingly embedded across workflows: tutoring support, content authoring, adaptive practice, student advising, academic integrity processes, and learning analytics.

title: Beyond the Compute Trap: The True Moat in Enterprise AI Lies in the "Macro-Symbolic Layer" and Digital Sovereignty

detail.title: Beyond the Compute Trap: The True Moat in Enterprise AI Lies in the "Macro-Symbolic Layer" and Digital Sovereignty
detail.abstract:
The prevailing narrative in AI assumes that scaling foundation models will inherently resolve enterprise safety and compliance challenges. This paper argues the opposite: as large language models develop sophisticated internal reasoning, the need for an external, deterministic governance layer becomes more urgent, not less. We introduce the distinction between observability and governability, demonstrating that even full transparency into a model’s chain of thought does not enable deterministic intervention in its runtime behavior. Drawing on zero-tolerance regulatory frameworks across aviation, finance, and healthcare, alongside emerging global legislation including the EU AI Act, U.S. Executive Order 14110, and China’s Interim Measures for Generative AI, we establish that the statistical constraints inherent to neural networks—including those provided by techniques such as Constitutional AI—are structurally insufficient for mission-critical environments. We propose the Macro-Symbolic Layer: an independent, model-agnostic control plane that enforces deterministic architectural rules at the input and output boundaries of probabilistic AI systems, using formal symbolic constructs rather than
ambiguous natural language. We further argue that this layer constitutes the locus of enterprise Digital Sovereignty—an organization’s non-negotiable right to retain full ownership of its governance logic, safety boundaries, and experiential assets independent of any model vendor. Analyzing architectural decoupleability, immunity to model behavioral drift, vertical experience encoding, cognitive network effects, and build-versus-buy economics, we position the Macro-Symbolic Layer as a distinct and defensible infrastructure category in the emerging enterprise AI stack.

title: News Behind the News: Spillover Effects of AI Crawler Blocking Among News Publishers

detail.abstract: The emergence of generative AI has intensified long-standing tensions between content producers and platforms over the value of online content. We examine how news organizations responded to this shift by analyzing historical robots.txt snapshots from the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, constructing a monthly panel of news publishers across the United States, Europe, and the Rest of the World from May 2022 through December 2025. Using Interrupted Time Series and Callaway-Sant'Anna staggered difference-indifferences designs, we study publisher responses to the release of GPTBot in August 2023. We document three main findings. First, blocking accelerated after GPTBot's release across all three regions, with U.S. and European publishers increasing blocking at similar rates and more strongly than publishers in the Rest of the World. Second, paywalled outlets block more quickly and more strongly than free outlets. Third, blocking extended beyond AI-related crawlers: GPTBot blocking was followed by increased blocking of non-AI bots, with the strongest evidence of this spillover in the U.S. and Europe. These findings suggest that the rise of generative AI has contributed to a broader tightening of automated web access among news publishers, with implications extending beyond AI training to the governance of crawling on the web.

title: Agents for Experiments, Experiments for Agents: A Design Grammar for AI-enabled Experimental Science
affiliations: Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business and Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Agents for Experiments, Experiments for Agents: A Design Grammar for AI-enabled Experimental Science
detail.abstract: AI systems are becoming active participants in organizational and knowledge work. They increasingly interact with humans, coordinate workflows, and operate in multi-agent arrangements. Understanding their effects therefore requires more than measuring output accuracy; it requires evidence about mechanisms, delegation, feedback, and control. Experiments remain central to this task, but they also face a recursive challenge: we need experiments for agents to study these arrangements, and we may need agents for experiments to help search the expanding space of possible designs. Yet experimental conditions for human-AI and agentic workflows are still largely specified in prose, making them difficult to compare, reuse, or audit. We frame this as a problem of workflow representation, traceability, and governance in AI-enabled knowledge production. We introduce SEED (Structural Encoding for Experimental Discovery), a framework that represents experimental conditions as typed actor-flow graphs. SEED supports three design functions: describing conditions as interaction structures, evaluating structural novelty relative to encoded prior designs, and generating candidate designs under feasibility and governance constraints. We report a lightweight empirical feasibility test that compares graph-blind and SEEDguided generation in a medical-triage design task. In this diagnostic contrast, SEED-guided candidate designs show clearer actor-flow changes, assumptions, and governance checks, supporting the feasibility of the grammar as a design aid. The commentary closes by identifying governance tensions around novelty, replication, validity, diversity of inquiry, and accountability.

title: The Shrinking Synthesis: Information-Technology Settlement Cycles and the 2037-2047 Window for AI's Institutional Reformation

detail.title: The Shrinking Synthesis: Information-Technology Settlement Cycles and the 2037-2047 Window for AI's Institutional Reformation
detail.abstract: Every major information-propagation technology follows the same five-phase cycle: diffusion, capture, chaos, foundational institutional response, and consolidation. Settlement timesmeasured from the onset of mass propagation to the first major non-anticipatory institutional response-have compressed from 249 years (printing press, 1440-1689) through 46 years (telegraph, 1844-1890) to a tightly clustered band of 20-25 years across radio, television, and the internet. The plateau is consistent with a generational-floor hypothesis: institutional adaptation cannot compress below the time required for a cohort to grow up with the technology as normal. This paper identifies the compression pattern across five Western cases plus a non-Western illustration and two held-out applications of the coding rule, proposes a mechanism rooted in institutional accumulation and cohort replacement, and offers a historically grounded hypothesis for artificial intelligence's settlement timeline: first major institutional response in the 2037-2047 window, derived from the empirical clustering of the last three cycles and triangulated with cohort-replacement arithmetic for the AI Early-Formative-Partial-Exposure cohort whose plasticity windows encompass ChatGPT's 2022 onset. The prediction is a falsifiable structural extrapolation, not a quantitative forecast, with pre-registered conditions: settlement before 2037 disconfirms the floor mechanism (one generation from diffusion onset); settlement after 2049 disconfirms the compression thesis. AI's material differences-its dual nature as information and productivity technology, structural limits on classical capture under globalisation, and the novelty of anticipatory regulation-create prediction uncertainty. The horizon is policy-actionable: longer than electoral cycles but within a generation, it defines when coordinated institutional design is possible.

title: Preference Revelation under Design Frictions: Evidence from Cookie Consent Banners

detail.title: Preference Revelation under Design Frictions: Evidence from Cookie Consent Banners

Additional research funds were provided by the Behavioral Law and Economics Research Group at the Max Planck Institute for Research on Collective Goods.

detail.abstract:
Privacy law relies on notice-and-consent regimes to govern data collection. This is premised on the idea that observed consent reflects users' underlying privacy preferences. Because consent is supposed to function as an informational signal, law assigns it the role of authorizing data collection. In practice, however, consent interfaces can make some options easier to recognize or implement than others, introducing asymmetric refusal costs that degrade the signal content of observed choices. We study this in a preregistered online experiment with German internet users (n= 1,142). Holding information and the formal option set constant, we vary cookie banner designs that differ in how refusal is presented: one visually emphasizes acceptance, one places rejection behind a settings menu, and one embeds the rejection option as a low-salience text link. We relate consent choices to privacy preferences measured via the IUIPC-8 scale, examining both the level of consent and the mapping from preferences to observed behavior. 

     We find that users with stronger privacy concerns are consistently less likely to accept cookies across all designs. Two of the three designs generate large increases in acceptance relative to a neutral baseline; purely visual emphasis does not. We find no evidence that any design systematically weakens the preference-consent relationship. The dominant pattern is threshold relocation: interfaces shift aggregate acceptance through refusal-side costs without distorting preference-based ordering. To interpret heterogeneity across designs, we distinguish execution costs from recognition costs as distinct channels through which interface design shapes consent. Execution frictions primarily affect users with weaker privacy concerns; recognition frictions shift acceptance broadly, including among users with strong concerns. This distinction helps organize divergent findings across studies and has direct implications for evaluating consent as a signal of user preferences and for regulatory standards governing interface design.

title: AI and Productivity: The Impact of ChatGPT's Release on Blogging
affiliations: University of Houston, University of Houston - Department of Decision & Information Sciences and University of Notre Dame

detail.title: AI and Productivity: The Impact of ChatGPT's Release on Blogging
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the fastest-growing technologies in history, offering innovative tools that can enhance worker productivity. In this paper, we examine the influence of ChatGPT's release on the output of workers who adopt it in a quasi-experiment. We study the productivity, popularity, and novelty of bloggers and their work on Medium.com. Popularity and novelty reflect productive efforts to engage one's readers and expand the scope of one's work, respectively. We measure AI use with the least biased detection tool available at the time of this study. We use Coarsened Exact Matching to match ChatGPT-adopters with similar bloggers who do not adopt. We then perform a difference-in-difference analysis around ChatGPT's release using this sample. On average, ChatGPT's release increases the productivity of adopters and increases the novelty of their work but decreases its popularity. Further, the way that ChatGPT is used determines the impact on output. Bloggers with a large number of followers tend to use ChatGPT as a researching tool to create work on new topics, increasing the novelty of their work but at the cost of lower popularity. While tech-savvy bloggers adopt ChatGPT as a writing tool, increasing their productivity but not affecting their work's popularity nor novelty. Finally, the effect on productivity is persistent over the three months following ChatGPT's release.

detail.abstract: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's digital transformation under Vision 2030 depends on a workforce capable of designing, operating, and governing cloud-native enterprise platforms that integrate enterprise resource planning systems, large-scale data infrastructure, and artificial intelligence services. Recent companion work has set out reference architectures and migration strategies for these platforms; the present paper addresses the workforce capability that those architectures and strategies assume. The paper proposes a capability framework structured around four layers (foundational, platform, integration, and governance) and maps the framework to recognised international skills standards including the Skills Framework for the Information Age and the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education Workforce Framework. The paper situates the capability framework in the Saudi institutional landscape, including the Human Resources Development Fund, Tuwaiq Academy, the Saudi Data and AI Authority Academy, the National Cybersecurity Authority's training initiatives, and the Human Capability Development Program under Vision 2030. The paper draws on the author's earlier research on soft skills training for technology professionals to argue that workforce readiness is not a purely technical question and that the interpersonal and organisational dimensions are essential complements to technical depth. The contribution complements three companion papers on hybrid cloud reference architecture, cloud migration strategy, and cloud-native AI and big data integration, and forms part of a coherent body of work on cloud-era enterprise platforms for public-sector digital transformation.

detail.abstract: Enterprise SAP landscapes in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia face a multi-year migration to SAP S/4HANA, driven by the convergence of vendor support timelines, the cloud direction of national policy under Saudi Vision 2030, and the practical limits of legacy database platforms. The migration is rarely a single event; it is a sequenced programme that combines operating-system and database migration, brownfield conversion or greenfield implementation, and a target deployment pattern on cloud or hybrid infrastructure. The literature treats each of these elements in isolation, and the vendor documentation describes them from a single perspective. This paper proposes a consolidated migration strategy that integrates OS/DB migration to SAP HANA, the conversionversus-implementation decision for S/4HANA, near-zero-downtime techniques, and cloud-target deployment patterns into a coherent decision framework. The strategy is structured around six decision points, each with explicit inputs, outputs, and risk considerations, and is grounded in the SAP Activate methodology, the AWS Well-Architected SAP Lens, NIST cloud guidance, and the Saudi regulatory perimeter set by the Communications, Space and Technology Commission and the National Cybersecurity Authority. The paper presents a comparison of the principal migration approaches, discusses programme-level execution considerations, and identifies open questions for subsequent work. The contribution complements an earlier paper on hybrid cloud reference architecture for SAP and forms part of a wider portfolio on cloud-era enterprise platforms for public-sector digital transformation.

detail.abstract: Mobile banking has developed as a disruptive digital financial service capable of enhancing technological inclusion, especially in rural and marginalized populations. Even though mobile phones are widely used in South Africa, the successful optimization of mobile banking services in rural areas is still constrained by differences in infrastructure, digital literacy, socioeconomic situations, and trust. In order to determine and synthesize the factors impacting the optimization of mobile banking for technological inclusion in rural South Africa, this study performs a systematic literature review (SLR). In accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 475 peer-reviewed articles published from 2021 to 2025 were obtained from ScienceDirect, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, and IEEE Xplore. Following thorough screening and eligibility evaluation, 43 studies were incorporated into the final synthesis. Thematic study identified principal determinants categorized as technological infrastructure, system usability and dependability, privacy and security issues, motivational access, cultural impacts, accessibility limitations, and socioeconomic aspects. The results show that mobile banking makes a big difference in bringing people into the world of money and technology. But to make it work best in rural areas, we need a combined approach that addresses problems with infrastructure, digital literacy, trust-building, and cost. This review gives a strong theoretical base for creating context-specific optimization models that will increase the use of mobile banking and help reach larger goals for digital inclusion in rural South Africa.

detail.abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly critical for economic participation, service delivery, and social inclusion. In Nepal, rapid mobile and broadband expansion coexist with substantial disparities in digital access and usage. This study develops a digital readiness typology using individual-level data from the Global Findex 2025 dataset, identifying three groups: Digitally Ready, Digitally Excluded, and Digitally Emerging. The typology integrates mobile ownership, internet use, digital activities, and connectivity intensity, offering a nuanced perspective beyond single-access indicators. Analyses show that age and education strongly influence digital readiness, with younger and more educated individuals overrepresented in the Digitally Ready cluster. Digital readiness also facilitates digital financial inclusion: while traditional bank accounts are widespread, mobile money adoption is concentrated among Digitally Ready individuals, whereas Emerging and Excluded groups remain largely disconnected. These findings highlight the need for policies that combine infrastructure expansion with digital literacy and targeted financial inclusion initiatives.

title: Preregistration for Experiments with AI Agents
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Preregistration for Experiments with AI Agents

contentType.other: Accepted at ICML 2026 as a Spotlight (Top 5%) Position Paper

detail.abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and autonomous AI agents has given rise to a rapidly growing methodological paradigm: "in silico" behavioral experiments. Originally conceived as a way to use AI agents as proxies for human participants in studies of cognition, decision-making, and social dynamics, this approach has taken on new significance—as AI agents increasingly negotiate, transact, and make consequential decisions on behalf of people and organizations, understanding their behavior has become a research priority in its own right. While these experiments with AI agents offer unprecedented advantages in terms of scalability, cost efficiency, and experimental control, they also inherit, and in some cases amplify, methodological vulnerabilities that have long plagued human subjects research. To address these issues, this paper argues that preregistration practices—central to improving the credibility of human subjects experiments—should now be extended to experiments with AI agents. We systematically catalog the researcher degrees of freedom that experiments with AI agents introduce—model selection, prompt wording, settings, and outcome-contingent redesign, for example—and show how the low cost of iteration and lack of reporting norms make these choices both easy to exploit and difficult to detect. We propose a preregistration template tailored to experiments with AI agents and call on conferences, journals, and funding agencies to make preregistration standard practice for this emerging research paradigm.

detail.title: Endogenous Misinformation and Source Authentication

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have nothing to disclose.

detail.abstract: We study endogenous information provision and source authentication when secondary senders can copy primary senders' signals, providing a microfoundation for correlation neglect. Authentication mitigates this duplication bias but hinders information diffusion, creating ambiguous effects on misinformation and welfare. Crucially, we show that policies aimed at maximizing user welfare can be fundamentally misaligned with the goal of minimizing misinformation. Non-verification can be optimal when diffusion is highly valued or primary senders hold strong bargaining power. While factors like signal quality reduce misinformation under exogenous verification, the effects are uneven when verification is endogenous. We also examine intellectual property protection and self-regulation, consistently highlighting a core trade-off between information accuracy and diffusion in shaping platform policy and welfare outcomes.

title: The Impact of AI Search on the Online Content Ecosystem: Evidence from Google and Reddit
affiliations: Emory University - Goizueta Business School, Emory University - Information Systems and Operations Management and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: The Impact of AI Search on the Online Content Ecosystem: Evidence from Google and Reddit
detail.abstract: Search engines traditionally complement online content platforms by directing users seeking information to external websites. The emergence of generative AI search tools that summarize answers directly on the results page may disrupt this relationship by making visits to source platforms optional. We study this question using Google AI Overviews and Reddit, one of the largest online discussion platforms. Our identification exploits Google's content moderation policy: Safe-for-Work (SFW) Reddit communities are indexed by Google organic search and surfaced in Google AI Overviews, while Not-Safe-for-Work (NSFW) communities, though indexed by organic search, are prohibited from being referenced in AI Overview summaries. Using a difference-indifferences design, we find that AI Overviews increase engagement in SFW communities: daily comments rise by 12.0 percent and the number of commenting users by 12.3 percent relative to NSFW communities. The effects are concentrated in experience-based discussions (opinions, advice, and personal experiences) rather than fact-based information. However, the subsequent introduction of Google AI Mode, which allows users to interact conversationally with the AI summary, largely eliminates these gains in experience-based content. These results suggest that the effects of AI search depend critically on interface design and types of content.

title: Coal Mining, Child Health, and the Resource Curse: Evidence from China ​
affiliations: Nanjing Audit University, Tohoku University - Graduate School of Economics & Management and Nanjing Audit University

detail.title: Coal Mining, Child Health, and the Resource Curse: Evidence from China ​
detail.abstract: This paper examines an underexplored channel of the resource curse by studying how coal mining affects water quality and child health in China. We construct a novel panel dataset linking the staggered opening of coal mines to firm-level pollution discharge, surface water quality, and household-level child health outcomes from 2010 to 2014. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that new coal mine openings significantly worsen local water quality and harm child health. Exposure to a new mine increases the probability of child illness by 8.2 percentage points and the number of sick days by 0.08 per month. Evidence on mechanisms points to water pollution as the main pathway. Although coal mining raises local income, these economic gains are insufficient to offset the associated health costs. We further show that stronger public policy and greater parental presence help mitigate these adverse effects. Overall, the findings show how environmental externalities from extraction can erode early-life health human capital, suggesting that the resource curse can be mitigated through targeted policies and social support for mining-area households. ​

detail.abstract: This paper shows the declining trend in internal migration in the United States is primarily due to increasing home attachment in “fast locations,” areas with relatively high rates of population turnover. These locations were population growth destinations in the 20th century, with transient populations that settled as regional population growth converged. The qualitative patterns of the U.S. experience can be generated by a model of location choice in heterogeneous regions with overlapping generations when the population has a home bias that varies endogenously with the history of population change. Using a novel measure of home attachment, this paper estimates a structural model of migration that distinguishes moving frictions from home utility. Simulations quantify channels of the mobility decline. Rising home attachment accounts for much of the decline, predominantly in fast locations. Population aging explains most of the remainder but in a more spatially neutral way.

detail.title: MagTetris+: A fast simulator for magnetic field and force calculation for ferromagnetic materials and permanent magnets
detail.abstract: Permanent magnet array is a popular option for low-field portable magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to generate the main magnetic field for polarization because it does not require large power supply nor a cooling system. A typical magnet array consists of permanent magnets and ferromagnetic components, such as shims and yokes. The conventional simulation of a permanent magnet array uses Finite-Element-Method (FEM) to solve maxwell equations. Although widely accepted as the standard for simulation accuracy, FEM is time-consuming and memory intensive, hindering research and development progress, especially for labs operating in resource-scarce regions without high-performance computing hardware. In this manuscript, a rapid and memory efficient simulator for magnet array consisting of both ferromagnetic materials and permanent magnets is proposed. To build the simulator, physics-based formulation with heuristics and stabilization term is proposed. It’s accuracy is validated against FEM-based results and proven to possess rapid computation and higher memory efficiency.
